### B364017 — The regression report on the placement gesture: REFUTED, and the instrument now answers the question itself `[Notes / Testing]` (bug) #notes #testing #ui  *(owner chat block, 2026-08-11 — STILL BROKEN #2, filed fairly by the reporter as a COMPARATIVE result with the caveat stated: "synthetic events do not move the native caret… but this is the same instrument, the same page shape, the same coordinates". Minted **B364017** from this branch's reserved block B364016–B364031 against origin/main 73c5011. **DEDUPE-FIRST** — this is the MOUSE edition of the repo's own **SYNTHETIC-KEYS-DONT-EDIT** rule, which covers the keyboard and is guarded by `verify-delete-drive`; filed as its own item because the mouse had no such guard and the gap cost a false regression report on a working feature.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-11 — the feature works with a real mouse, and the verdict table is now measured every run instead of being folklore.**
- Verify: sandbox — `ui-audit/verify-notes-anchor-soak.mjs` **32/32** on the reported build · `ui-audit/verify-press-drive.mjs` 6/6.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-11 from chat.
- **THE ANSWER IS THAT IT WORKS.** The real-input soak places a block at every point across three window sizes on the exact build the report was made against. Nothing regressed.
- **⛔ AND THE CAUSE OF THE FALSE NEGATIVE IS ONE WORD: the placement moved from `dblclick` to `mousedown` in that same shipment.** A driver dispatching a synthetic `click` or `dblclick` produces **no `mousedown` at all**, so it reaches nothing — with the right element under the cursor and the editor focused. Every symptom of a broken feature and none of the cause. That is why the result was comparative: the instrument was correct an hour earlier and the door it was knocking on had moved.
- **THE MEASURED TABLE, re-measured on every run by `verify-press-drive.mjs`** (aimed at the same element for every row, so a "no" is about the event and never about the aim):

  | how the press was made | result |
  |---|---|
  | the driver's real `mouse.click` | **places a block** |
  | the driver's real `mouse.dblclick` | **places a block** (press 2 lands inside what press 1 made) |
  | synthetic `click`, bubbling | does nothing |
  | synthetic `dblclick`, bubbling | does nothing — **the shape that produced the report** |
  | synthetic `mousedown`, `bubbles: false` | does nothing |
  | synthetic `mousedown`, `bubbles: true` | **places a block** |

- **⛔ SO THE FIX IS A GUARD, NOT A CODE CHANGE.** The run FAILS if the measured table stops matching the documented one, so the day the wiring moves again this says so — instead of a harness quietly reporting a working feature as broken, or a broken one as working. `ui-audit/lib/pressFeature.mjs` is the supported driver and **throws rather than reporting a pass it did not earn**, the same discipline `deleteFeature.mjs` follows for the keyboard.
- **For any harness that needs it:** use the real mouse, or dispatch `mousedown` with `bubbles: true`.

### B364018 — A conflict prompt on a note nobody edited: the two copies differed only by empty blocks `[Notes]` (bug) #notes #sync #ui  *(owner chat block, 2026-08-11 — the "ALSO, FOR AWARENESS" item, raised without a demand and correctly left unresolved because it is his data: "a conflict appearing on a note nobody edited is worth a look". Minted **B364018** from this branch's reserved block. **DEDUPE-FIRST** — **B1391** built the quiet-settle path (`judgeConflict`) that stops a moved REVISION being reported as a disagreement, and this is a second class of non-disagreement it did not know about; filed as its own number rather than a B1391 recurrence because B1391's rule is intact and correct.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-11 — and it was a real conflict, which is why it is worth naming.**
- Verify: sandbox — `test/notesBinPurge.test.js`, five cases including both directions and three ways it must still fire.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-11 from chat.
- **WHAT HE SAW.** *"“Load Study” also changed in another of your windows. Nothing was overwritten — pick which to keep."* on a note he had not touched.
- **THE CAUSE, and it is this shipment's own doing.** The one-time clean-up announced *"Cleared 10 empty boxes left behind by an earlier version, across 1 note."* One window had cleaned that note; the other still had the ten empty blocks. The copies genuinely differed — **by exactly the objects the app itself has decided are worthless and is deleting everywhere.**
- **⛔ THE RULE: AN EMPTY BLOCK CANNOT BE THE SUBSTANCE OF A DISAGREEMENT.** Asking somebody to choose between "the copy with ten invisible empty boxes" and "the copy without" is not a decision. `judgeConflict` now compares the two copies with the litter discounted — the same reasoning `canonNode` already applies to a null attribute, which is the difference between *the bytes differ* and *the note differs*. The CLEAN copy wins and stays owed to the cloud, so the litter leaves the account instead of being kept in silence on whichever side happened to have it.
- **⛔ AND IT MUST STILL FIRE ON A REAL ONE**, which is the half that would be easy to lose: an edit to the words, an edit made INSIDE a block, and a block holding a picture are all still genuine disagreements and are all asserted.

Minted **B357008** from this branch's reserved block B357008–B357023 against origin/main af0d914. **DEDUPE-FIRST** — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `anchor`, `noteAnchor`, `placeAnchor`, `empty`, `provisional`, `intermittent`, `B1393`, `B342993`, `B350000`, `B350001`, `B350004`: **B350000/B350001** fixed WHERE a block lands and proved it at 38 positions — that work is intact and this is not a recurrence of it; **B350004** fixed a press inside a block with WORDS in it, and an EMPTY one is the case it could not reach, because there is no text for the browser to put a caret on. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-11 — 32/32 in a new soak harness across three window sizes, and mutation-proven at the seam.**
- Verify: sandbox — `ui-audit/verify-notes-anchor-soak.mjs` 32/32 · `test/notesAnchorPrune.test.js` 21 cases.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-11 from chat.
- **THE MEASUREMENT.** Five double-clicks on a scratch page with nothing typed: all five were written to storage as `noteAnchor` nodes with x/y/w and no text, and all five survived a reload.
- **⛔ AND THAT LITTER *IS* THE INTERMITTENCY, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING.** An empty block draws nothing you can see and **still occupies its box and still takes the press**. So the second attempt at a spot you already tried lands inside the first attempt's invisible leftover and appears to do nothing at all. It fails exactly where somebody already tried once and gave up — which is what *"it works intermittently"* turned out to mean. Two of the reporter's own double-clicks on apparently blank space produced nothing, both inside earlier empty blocks.
- **THE FIX IS THAT AN EMPTY BLOCK IS PROVISIONAL, ENFORCED AT THE STORAGE SEAM RATHER THAN IN THE GESTURE.** The editor removes one the moment the caret leaves it, on blur, and on Escape — that is what you SEE. `writePage` prunes any empty block on the way to the disk — that is what makes it TRUE, and it is what closes the doors a gesture-side fix leaves open: an autosave firing in the half-second before the first keystroke, a closed tab, a crash, a cloud push.
- **⛔ THE BAR FOR "EMPTY" IS A WHITELIST AND REFUSES TO GUESS.** No text at all, and every node inside it a plain paragraph. A picture, an attachment, a sketch, a table, a heading — or **any node type this code has not heard of** — is content and is left alone. Unknown must mean keep.
- **AND AN EMPTY BLOCK IS NEVER INVISIBLE.** It is outlined while it is empty and says "Type here" while the caret is in it, driven by the SAME predicate the storage seam uses — two definitions would mean a block that looks provisional and is kept, or looks real and is thrown away.
- **A ONE-TIME CLEAN-UP** goes through every stored note on load and rewrites only the ones actually carrying empty blocks, through `writePage` so the cleaned copy reaches the cloud too, and says so on screen rather than doing it quietly.
- **PANEL-BREVITY:** no panel copy touched.

### B270913 — Retention on `client_errors`: the owner asked me to pick the number, I picked it, and it is APPLIED — 90 days ordinary, ONE YEAR for his manual captures `[Platform / Infra]` (task) #infra #persistence #perf  *(filed 2026-08-08 as a PROPOSAL under his explicit "propose it with a number and let him decide; do not apply one". **DECIDED AND SHIPPED 2026-08-09** on his follow-up, verbatim: *"if it makes sense that we should let's do it, I don't know a good number though so u come up with it."* **DEDUPE-FIRST: this re-uses B270913 and mints NO new number** — it is the same item reaching its decision point, which is what the item was opened for. **B270912** remains the RATE fix and is untouched; **B1427/B1429** are the device-storage tier, a different store entirely.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-10 — V84560 PASSED. The job fires unattended, and has now done so on two consecutive days.**
- **DISPOSITION, NAMED: (a) IMPLEMENT IT AND VERIFY IT LIVE.** Not "instrument it and wait", not "ask him whether it is gone" — the policy was written, applied to production, and then observed working on its own schedule against the real table. Nothing here is closed on a null.
- **⛔ THE STOPPING RULE THIS ITEM CARRIED WAS MET, WITH MARGIN, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY THAT MATTERS.** The rule was: *closes when V84560 records a run row that nobody triggered, appearing on the schedule with `status = ok`.* Two such rows exist — **2026-08-09 07:20:00.188** and **2026-08-10 07:20:00.219**, both `ordinary_deleted 0 · manual_deleted 0`, table unchanged at 5,400 and 5,435 — and pg_cron's own independent ledger confirms both from the other side (`cron.job_run_details`: two runs, both `succeeded`, `return_message: "1 row"`). Consecutive days, so it is not a single lucky fire. `client_errors_retention_status` reads **`ok`**.
- **AND `0` DELETED IS THE POINT, NOT A DISAPPOINTMENT.** 0 of 5,435 rows are eligible and none will be until **2026-09-18**. Before this item, *"the job ran and found nothing"* and *"the job never ran"* produced the identical observation for months. They now produce different rows, and the status view names which one you have. The check that closed this was written so the manual proof run (id 1) could NOT satisfy it, and `prune_client_errors()` was deliberately **not** called by hand during verification — a hand-triggered run writes a byte-identical row and would have destroyed the only evidence the check existed to gather.
- **Re-confirmed in the same pass:** the owner's two rows from 2026-08-07 19:07:38 (`event:stale-cache-overruled` / `event:element-rows-canonical`, Sylvestri `sms4zs8unbkg`) are still present, and the table's oldest row is unmoved at 2026-06-20 22:16:28.
- Verify: live → **V84560 PASSED 2026-08-10** ·
- Origin: filed 2026-08-08 from chat · decided + applied 2026-08-09 from chat
- **⛔ THE NUMBERS, AND WHY EACH ONE.**
  - **90 DAYS for an ordinary row.** Re-measured against production this session: **5,279 rows · oldest 2026-06-20 · 0 of them older than 90 days.** So switching this on **deletes nothing today** — it cannot lose him anything now, and it only begins trimming as the table naturally ages. That is the property that makes 90 the safe number rather than the aggressive one: the policy arrives with zero cost and zero effect, and earns its keep later.
  - **365 DAYS for a perf capture whose `kind` is `manual`.** A manual capture is him personally pressing *"that felt slow just now"* — the rarest and highest-value row in the table, and there will only ever be a handful. The value of one is comparing a symptom to the same symptom a season ago, which a 90-day window destroys. Keeping them four times longer costs nothing measurable.
- **⛔ THE GUARD MATTERS MORE THAN THE POLICY, AND THAT IS THE OWNER'S OWN FRAMING.** A retention job that silently never runs is INDISTINGUISHABLE from one that correctly had nothing to delete — and because this policy is a no-op against today's data, that is not hypothetical, **it is the expected state for months.** That is the sixth appearance of this exact class here (the swallowing sink · the frame-count sustain window · the packed track that emptied on real stalls · the drift gate's invented fixture · the perf metrics that stayed muted after their cause was gone). So:
  - **Every run writes a row to `public.client_errors_retention_runs` — INCLUDING a run that deleted nothing.** The insert is deliberately not inside an `if deleted > 0`. A 0/0 row is an **empty report**; no row at all is an **absent** one; those mean opposite things and the schema makes them different objects.
  - **`public.client_errors_retention_status` answers which one you are looking at in one word:** `never-run` (the job has never proven itself — treat as broken, NOT as clean) · `stale` (ran once, then stopped — two missed days on a daily schedule) · `ok`. Beside it, `last_total_deleted = 0` is a healthy no-op and reads as one.
  - Each run row also carries the **cutoffs it used** and `rows_before` / `rows_after`, so a reader never has to guess which version of the policy ran.
- **⛔ THE TEST RUNS THE SHIPPED SQL FILE, VERBATIM, AGAINST A REAL POSTGRES — not a JS re-implementation of the predicate.** `test/clientErrorsRetention.test.js` (21) reads `client_errors.sql` and `client_errors_retention.sql` off disk and executes them into **PGlite** (Postgres compiled to WASM — real planner, real regex, real interval arithmetic; added as a **devDependency only**, so it is charged against no client bundle). The only thing stubbed is what Supabase provides and a bare Postgres does not: `auth.uid()` and the `anon` / `authenticated` roles. A test that re-implemented the rule in JS would be testing its own copy, which this repo has been caught doing.
  - **BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is what he asked for:** an ordinary row at 100 days is **REMOVED** while a **manual capture of the SAME age SURVIVES**. Eleven seeded cases, one assertion each, plus an exact set-equality so nothing outside the policy can move unnoticed. An **AUTO** capture is a control and correctly takes the ordinary window — it is not his press.
  - **MUTATION-CHECKED, both clauses.** Delete the `not is_manual_perf_capture(...)` carve-out from the loaded SQL and the manual capture dies at 90 days. Widen `interval '90 days'` to 400 and the stale ordinary row survives. Without those, a predicate matching nothing at all would pass the happy path by accident.
  - Also asserted: the no-op run still logs · `never-run` vs `ok` vs `stale` · idempotence (a second run deletes nothing more and still logs) · and a **malformed capture payload cannot take the run down** — which is why the classifier is a regex and not a `::jsonb` cast, since a cast RAISES and one bad row would abort the whole nightly delete.
- **APPLIED TO PRODUCTION 2026-08-09** (`lyeqzkuiwngunutlkkmi`, migration `client_errors_retention_b270913`). `pg_cron` installed; job **`planyr-client-errors-retention`**, schedule **`20 7 * * *`** (07:20 UTC — inside his overnight, and off the hour so it does not contend with everything else that runs at :00), command `select public.prune_client_errors()`, active, owned by `postgres`. Immediately after apply, `client_errors_retention_status` read **`never-run`** — correct, and the point of that state existing.
- **AND IT WAS PROVEN ON THE REAL TABLE, not just in the sandbox.** A single transaction seeded three rows tagged `B270913-live-proof` at 200 days old (one ordinary, one `kind:"manual"` capture, one `kind:"auto"` capture), ran `prune_client_errors()`, and asserted six things — the ordinary row gone · the **manual capture kept** · exactly 2 ordinary deletes (the react + auto rows) · 0 manual deletes · and **`rows_after = rows_before + 1`, i.e. no real row was touched**. It then deleted the surviving proof row itself. Recorded run: **`ordinary_deleted 2 · manual_deleted 0 · 5,288 → 5,286 · 3 ms`**. Table back to **5,285**, unchanged from before the proof. ⚠ Read run #1 in the log as exactly that — a proof, not a production trim.
- **⛔ NOTHING OUTSIDE THE POLICY WAS TOUCHED.** No read-side filter, no truncation, no "while we're here" cleanup. **His two rows from 2026-08-07 19:07:38** — `event:stale-cache-overruled` and `event:element-rows-canonical` on his real Sylvestri plan (`sms4zs8unbkg`) — were confirmed present before the change and confirmed present after; they are ordinary rows well inside 90 days, ineligible by construction, and a genuine record of the app self-healing his data.
- **HONEST LIMIT, stated rather than left to be discovered:** `never-run` / `stale` is *queryable*, and nothing *polls* it. There is no ops dashboard in this product and building one is not in this item's scope. So the reader is a human running one query — which is what **V84560** was, and what its stopping rule was written against. **That limit still stands after the pass:** the job is proven to fire, but nothing polls the status view, so a future stoppage would be silent until someone looks. The mitigation is that the state is now *representable and named* rather than inferred — which is the difference between a question someone can answer in one query and one that needs an investigation.
- **STOPPING RULE.** This closes when V84560 records a run row that **nobody triggered**, appearing on the schedule with `status = ok`. If tomorrow's read still says `never-run`, the job is not firing and this re-opens HERE with a `Recurrence:` line — a scheduled job that never runs is precisely the failure this item's whole guard half exists to make visible, and it would be absurd to let it hide inside the item that built the detector.
- **SUPERSEDED, and recorded so the file does not contradict itself:** the 2026-08-08 recommendation on this item was *"NOT YET — revisit at ~50,000 rows or ~50 MB, then 365 days"*. The owner asked for a number now, and the reasoning that changed is that **a 90-day window costs nothing today** (0 eligible rows), so "wait until it matters" and "apply it now" have the same effect on his data this year — while applying it now means the machinery, and its liveness guard, are in place and PROVEN before the first row is ever eligible. The 365-day figure survives, narrowed to the class it was actually argued for: his manual captures.

### B342993 — Double-click in blank page space starts a block WHERE YOU CLICKED `[Notes]` (bug ×4) #notes #ui  *(owner chat block, 2026-08-10 — fourth report)*
`[x]` A real positioned node, not an emulation. Proven geometrically.
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-08-10 from chat (NEW-2).
- **THE PREVIOUS ROUND VERIFIED THE WRONG PROPERTY, and the owner said so.** It confirmed the old alignment hack was gone and that text landed left-aligned at the END OF THE DOCUMENT — and passed. Landing at the end of the document IS the reported bug. The round before asserted the caret took FOCUS, which was also true while the text appeared on line one.
- **SO THE ANSWER IS A REAL NODE (`noteAnchor`), NOT PADDING PARAGRAPHS PLUS TEXT-ALIGN.** The position is two numbers ON the node, which makes every previous failure structurally impossible: it cannot crawl as you type, cannot leak an alignment onto the next paragraph, leaves nothing to backspace through, persists and syncs because it IS the document, prints in place (PDF-PARITY — `renderHTML` writes the offsets, so paper and screen read the same two numbers), and can be dragged afterwards.
- **TWO THINGS LEARNED THE HARD WAY, both in the file header:** the block is inserted BEFORE the document's last block, because appending leaves a trailing empty paragraph ProseMirror restores and two attempts to delete it silently did nothing; and the mat's own press handler adds a line per press, so a double-click added two — counted and taken back in the same gesture.
- **THE CHECK IS GEOMETRIC.** `verify-notes-anchor-zoom` asserts the rendered rect against the clicked coordinates (**0 px off**, and still 0 px off while zoomed), plus: it does not move while typing, no padding paragraphs, the existing line unchanged, it survives a reload, dragging moves it and WRITES the new position, and double-click-to-select-a-word still works.

### B342994 — Ctrl+zoom in Notes `[Notes]` (feature) #notes #ui  *(owner chat block, 2026-08-10)*
`[x]` Ctrl+wheel and Ctrl+= / Ctrl+- / Ctrl+0 scale the document.
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-08-10 from chat (NEW-3).
- Scales the **document**, never the app chrome or the rail — the browser already scales everything together; what it cannot do is "make the writing bigger and leave my navigation where it is". The browser's own zoom is **suppressed** for these gestures (non-passive wheel listener + `preventDefault`), so the two cannot fight.
- CSS `zoom`, not a transform: the text must RE-WRAP at the new size and the caret must stay the browser's own — and it is what lets the anchored blocks of B342993 recover the live scale by measuring rather than by being told.
- Level persists **per scope** and deliberately does NOT sync (a comfortable size belongs to the screen you are sitting at). Ctrl+0 returns to 100%. The level is shown only when it is not 100%, and clicking it resets. **VIEWPORT-STABLE**: the scroll anchor is measured before the step and restored in a layout effect, before paint.

### B342995 — Delete confirmation counted the note itself as one of its own pages `[Notes]` (bug) #notes #ui  *(owner chat block, 2026-08-10)*
`[x]` "Delete 2?" for one page with one child.
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-08-10 from chat (NEW-4).
- **THE CAUSE, in one line:** `subtreePageIds` includes the node itself — correct for a DELETE, which needs every body to clear — and the confirmation rendered that same number. So a page with a single child announced "Delete 2?" and then "and its 2 pages".
- Now `descendantPageIds` + `subpagesPhrase`: **"Delete + 1 subpage?"** and **"…and its 1 subpage."** The delete's cascade is unchanged; only the number shown to a person moved.

Re-introducing it in copy would re-introduce it in people's heads. **Subpages** is the honest word at every depth; flagged here rather than silently diverged.

### B290251 — The mint gate reports a FALSE `TAKEN` on main's own ids after you follow CLAUDE.md's mandated conflict resolution `[Infra / Testing]` (task) #infra #testing  *(filed 2026-08-09 — hit while shipping the Colorado audit (#972), by doing exactly what `CLAUDE.md` → Workflow & deploy instructs. Minted from this branch's reserved block B290240–B290255. **DEDUPE-FIRST** — searched `check-mint`, `mint gate`, `B779`, `B1140`, `B6864`, `mintFatality`: B779 built the gate, B6864–B6867 replaced the high-water-mark rule with reserved blocks. This is neither of those verdicts misfiring — it is the "added by this branch" INPUT being wrong after a merge. New item.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-09 — the gate no longer reads main's own items as this branch's mints, and a genuine double-mint is still fatal (now in TWO places rather than one).**
- **THE FIX, and it is NOT the one-liner the costed plan proposed.** The plan's shape was `priorIds = union(onBase, onMain)` for the TAKEN test. **That would have silently deleted the B1140 case** — the whole reason the merge base is used — because in B1140 the id IS on main, so unioning it into `priorIds` exculpates exactly the collision the gate exists for. What shipped instead keeps `added` measured against the merge base and asks a second question of each id it flags: **is the heading here byte-identical to main's heading for that id?** Identical → the content came from main, advisory. Different → two features, one number, fatal, and the message now prints BOTH titles.
- **⛔ AUDIT-FIRST CORRECTED THE ITEM'S OWN DIAGNOSIS BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN.** Reproduced in a throwaway-repo lab: **a plain `git merge origin/main` was never affected at all** — the merge commit moves the merge base to main's tip, so main's ids stop being "added" by construction. The failing shape is a resolution that takes main's CONTENT without its ANCESTRY (`git merge --squash`, `git checkout origin/main -- BACKLOG.md`, a rebuilt branch), which is what leaves the base behind while the tree carries main's headings. An e2e arm exercising only a clean merge commit would have passed before the fix and proved nothing — so both arms exist, and the content-only one is the arm that goes red on the old code.
- **Measured, before → after, same lab, same four cases:** content-copy merge **3 fatal offenders → 0** · genuine double-mint, unmerged **fatal → fatal** · genuine double-mint after merging main **PASSED SILENTLY → fatal** · clean merge commit **clean → clean**.
- **THE THIRD CASE IS A BUG THIS ITEM DID NOT KNOW IT HAD.** Once a branch merges main, the base moves past the collision and the old gate had nothing left to see: an independently double-minted id sailed through the pre-push hook. It is now caught at push time by a duplicate-heading check (B308704) reusing the detector `test/idUniqueness.test.js` runs. **That is what makes the relaxation above safe rather than merely argued** — the check that was loosened and the check that was added cover each other.
- **Neither the merge-base reasoning nor the fatal-TAKEN verdict was weakened.** `test/mintFatality.test.js` is green: the fatal verdict is still a function of a present, proven collision and of no aggregate of peer state.
- Sandbox: `test/mintGuard.test.js` (+6 pure cases, incl. **RED when no heading evidence is supplied — exculpation must be earned, never granted by an empty map**) · `test/mintGateE2E.test.js` (+4 arms against real git refs in throwaway repos, both directions) · full suite 10,223 green.
- **A FIXTURE DEFECT THE NEW CASE EXPOSED, worth recording:** `writeBacklog` gave every scratch item the identical title `scratch item`, under which "main's item arrived here" and "two sessions minted one number" are genuinely indistinguishable. Case (a) passed for the wrong reason until the fixture modelled two different features as two different titles.
`[ ]` `npm run check-mint` measures "ids added by this branch" against the MERGE BASE, so after you merge `origin/main` into a branch to clear a conflict, every id main added since the base looks like this branch minted it — and the gate then calls each one `ALREADY TAKEN on origin/main` and blocks the push.
- Verify: sandbox
- **Measured, 2026-08-09.** Branch base `cf4f77b`, main tip `ae2ce02`. `git merge origin/main` (the resolution `CLAUDE.md` prescribes for a `dirty` PR — *"merging `origin/main` into the branch fixed it instantly"*) → the gate failed with **11 fatal offenders**: B280402, B280403, B280704–B280707, B286000, B286001, V78961, V79264, V84560. Each was verified to appear **exactly once** on `origin/main`, **exactly once** in the working tree (the same item, arrived via the merge), and **not at all at the merge base**. There was no duplicate heading anywhere in either file pair.
- **Why the input is wrong and the verdict is right.** `scripts/check-mint.mjs` computes `priorIds` from the merge base *(its own comment explains why — the B1140 case, where main merged an item under a number a branch was independently holding)*. That reasoning is sound and should not be undone. The gap is that it does not EXCLUDE ids reachable from `origin/main` itself: an id that is on main **and** whose content came from main is not something this branch minted.
- **Severity: it blocks the documented recovery path, so it is worse than it looks.** A stale PR needs a new push, a `dirty` PR swallows every nudge, and the fix for both is to merge main — which arms a pre-push hook AND a required build step against you. The obvious escape (renumbering) would be actively WRONG here: it would renumber *main's* items on this branch, creating the real duplicate the gate exists to prevent.
- **The route around, used on #972 and worth writing into `CLAUDE.md` either way: REBASE instead of merging.** `git rebase origin/main` makes the merge base main's tip, so only the branch's own ids read as added and the gate goes green with nothing renumbered. Costs a `--force-with-lease` push.
- **Costed plan — DO NOT BUILD blind; this is the mint gate and a wrong change here is expensive.** ~0.5 session. The one-line shape is `priorIds = union(onBase, onMain)` for the TAKEN test while keeping the base-only set for the peer-claim test — but that must be argued against B1140's case explicitly (does an id minted independently on BOTH sides still fail? It must), and `test/mintGateE2E.test.js` already drives all four outcomes against real git refs in throwaway repos, so the new case belongs there as a fifth arm proven red first. **Per `test/mintFatality.test.js`, whatever lands must keep the fatal verdict a function of a present, proven collision — never of an aggregate of peer state.**

`[x]` So a wrong stamp is visible at a glance.

### B308704 — 24 B numbers and 7 V numbers each name TWO different items INSIDE ONE ledger file, and nothing would have stopped the next one `[Infra / CI]` (bug) #infra #testing  *(filed 2026-08-09 from the owner's chat block, measured by him on `main` at ed7f8d3 and re-measured here. Minted **B308704** from this branch's reserved block B308704–B308719, against freshly-fetched `origin/main` ed7f8d3. **DEDUPE-FIRST** — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `duplicate`, `collision`, `uniqueness`, `KNOWN_LEGACY_ID_COLLISIONS`, `idUniqueness`, `B779`, `B780`, `B755`, `B1140`, `B6864`–`B6867`, `B36051`, `B290251`: **B780 is the closest and is explicitly NOT this** — it guards the CROSS-FILE pair and grandfathered 58 historical collisions, and these 31 were hiding INSIDE the permission that baseline had to grant. B779 guards the mint, B6864–B6867 made the numbers unraceable. Nothing owned same-file duplication. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-09 — every one of the 31 is disambiguated in place, and a same-file duplicate now fails the build.**
- Verify: sandbox — the whole item is ledger text and CI checks; no browser, no auth, no live data. Nothing to park.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-09 from the owner's chat block (Item B), shipped the same session.
- **THE MEASUREMENT, re-run here and matching his exactly:** 24 duplicate `### B` ids in **BACKLOG-DONE.md alone** and 7 duplicate `### V` ids in **VERIFICATION-DONE.md alone** — 63 headings across 31 numbers. `B127` is both *"Measure-type dropdown renders behind/clipped by the rail"* and *"Two-tab convergence: a stale tab could thin the durable store"*; `B239` is both *"Schedule module still dead-ends after a deploy"* and *"Restore the per-zone plus to add trailer parking"*. **Zero collisions among OPEN items** — `BACKLOG.md` and `VERIFICATION.md` are clean, so live work was never ambiguous and the damage is archive-only.
- **⛔ WHY THE TWO EXISTING GUARDS COULD NOT SEE IT, which is the actual defect.** `test/idUniqueness.test.js` checks the LIVE files (clean) and the live+archive PAIR against a grandfathered baseline. A count of two ACROSS THE PAIR is **ambiguous by design** — it is also the shape of a legitimate DEDUPE-FIRST recurrence caught mid-move — so that baseline had to be permissive, and 31 unambiguously-wrong ids sat inside the permission it granted. **Two headings for one id INSIDE A SINGLE FILE is never legitimate**: the lifecycle MOVES a heading between files, it never leaves two in one. That makes the new rule absolute, which is what lets it be a guard instead of another baseline to argue about.
- **THE BLOCKS DID WORK, and the item says so rather than implying a live crisis.** The colliding range is B127–B755, **entirely below B6864** — every one predates the reserved-block fix and **none has occurred since**. What nothing ever did was clean up the inheritance or stop the next one at the door.
- **⛔ THE DECISION: DISAMBIGUATE IN PLACE, NOT RENUMBER — and the reason is cross-references, not tidiness.** Prose across the repo says *"see B239"*. For a colliding id **nobody can know which twin a given reference meant** — that information was lost the day the second item took the number. Renumbering the later twin would silently repoint every such reference at the survivor, converting an ambiguity a reader can SEE into a wrong answer they cannot, and rewrite closed history to do it. So both twins keep the number and each gains a `> ⚠ SHARED ID` line naming the other (`scripts/mark-shared-ids.mjs`, idempotent and re-runnable).
- **THE CROSS-REFERENCE GUARANTEE, PROVEN AND NOT ASSERTED — the owner's explicit condition.** The repair is **purely additive**: `git diff --numstat` reads **49 / 0** and **14 / 0** — 63 insertions, **zero deletions, zero modified lines, zero non-marker additions**. Three standing proofs in `test/ledgerDuplicateIds.test.js` keep it that way: stripping every marker restores the file's id→heading-line map **exactly**; every marker's quoted twin title is re-checked against a real heading of that same id (63 markers examined, a count asserted so the proof cannot go vacuous); and the pure marker function is shown to preserve every original line in order. **Because no heading and no id changed, the resolution of every cross-reference in the repo — including the ones nobody has enumerated — is bit-for-bit what it was.** That is stronger than any survey of reference sites, because it does not depend on having found them all.
- **THE GUARD, which is the part that matters most.** `test/ledgerDuplicateIds.test.js` fails the build if any `### B#` / `### V#` heading appears twice **within one ledger file**, beyond a frozen, **shrink-only** baseline keyed `<file>::<id>` (so a dup cannot migrate between files unnoticed) and **restricted to the two ARCHIVE files** — a live-file duplicate is never grandfathered, at any count, and that stronger property is asserted directly. The same detector runs at PUSH time inside `check-mint.mjs`.
- **MUTATION-PROVEN, twice against the real ledger and not only in the abstract.** (1) A second `### B296224` appended to **BACKLOG.md** → **2 tests red** (`no NEW same-file B# duplicate`, `the LIVE files are completely clean`). (2) A second `### B1449` appended to **BACKLOG-DONE.md** — the historically real shape — → **2 tests red** (the new same-file check *and* B780's cross-file check). Both reverted; the ledgers are byte-identical to before the probe. Seven further mutation cases pin the boundaries: a grandfathered id collided one MORE time is red, the same grandfathered id duplicated in a DIFFERENT file is red, a recurrence spanning two files is green, a range heading is green, and the marker line itself must never read as a heading.
- Sandbox: `test/ledgerDuplicateIds.test.js` (18 cases) · `scripts/mark-shared-ids.mjs --check` · `npm run mark-shared-ids`.

### B298753 (×2) — Quick open did not take the keyboard, so typing went into the note behind it `[Notes]` (feature → bug) #notes #ui #persistence  *(originally filed 2026-08-09 from the owner's Tier-1 chat block; RE-OPENED the same day from his live verification of the merged build. DEDUPE-FIRST — this is a defect in the palette B298753 shipped, found on the build B298753 produced, so it takes the RECURRENCE treatment rather than a new number: anyone searching `quick open`, `Ctrl+K` or `QuickOpen.jsx` must land on ONE item carrying the whole story. Searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `focus`, `overlay`, `palette`, `activeElement`, `keydown`, `B1392`, `B1393`, `B36051`: no other item covers keyboard ownership of an overlay.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-09 (×2) — the palette claims the keyboard at the CHORD, not when it mounts. Nothing typed while it is open can reach the document, and nothing typed is lost either.**
- Verify: sandbox — reproduced HERE first, then fixed, then mutation-proven (ATTEMPT-BEFORE-YOU-PARK).
- Recurrence: 2026-08-09 — *"Ctrl+K opens the panel, but THE PANEL DOES NOT TAKE KEYBOARD FOCUS. I typed `Quadvest` and every character went into the NOTE behind the panel. The list never filtered. The word was written into his real Entitlements note, which had been empty."* **Data written into an owner's note by a feature that looks like a search box.**
- **⛔ THE MECHANISM, REPRODUCED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS CHANGED.** The chord only set React state; the PANEL claimed the keyboard by focusing its own field in a mount effect. Between those two moments nothing was claiming anything and the editor still had focus. The width of that gap is the whole bug: on a warm cache it is one React commit and **one character** leaks (measured: the `Q` of `Quadvest` landed in the document); on the FIRST Ctrl+K of a freshly-deployed build it is the download of the palette's lazy chunk, so **the whole word** leaks and the panel then appears showing an unfiltered list — which is exactly what he saw.
- **⛔ THE FIX DOES NOT DEPEND ON FOCUS, WHICH IS THE POINT.** A correctness property must not be a race with a chunk download, a React commit, and anything else that might take focus back. One window-level capture handler in `Notes.jsx` — the module that is ALREADY loaded — decides both things: it opens the palette on the chord and, from that same event onward, swallows every key not aimed at the palette. The open/closed flag is a **ref, flipped synchronously inside the event**, not state: an earlier version armed the swallow from a `useEffect` on `quickOpen` and still lost the first character to the commit it waited for.
- **⛔ AND SWALLOWED KEYS ARE BUFFERED INTO THE QUERY, NOT EATEN.** Discarding them would fix the data loss and leave the feature feeling broken — you type a name and nothing happens. Buffering puts every character where the person meant it to go, so typing straight through the chord filters the list before the panel has painted.
- **A SECOND, QUIETER BUG FOUND WHILE FIXING THE FIRST:** the panel called `select()` on mount. With an empty query that did nothing — but with a character buffered by the new gate it highlighted it, so the next keystroke replaced it and the field read `uadvest`. The caret goes to the END now; `select()` is gone.
- **Escape returns the caret to where it was.** The palette remembers `document.activeElement` before taking focus and restores it on close, so the next keystroke goes back into the note rather than to the page.
- **THE SAME CLASS ON THE OTHER TWO SURFACES, checked rather than assumed.** The **slash menu** is the deliberate opposite — its keystrokes are *supposed* to reach the document, because the `/h2` you type IS the filter and is removed when a command runs; what must not arrive as text is the navigation, and arrows/Escape are asserted inert. The **history pane** is a side pane that never takes focus, so typing while it is open must keep going to the note — a pane that quietly ate keystrokes would be the mirror image of this bug and just as invisible; asserted.
- **⛔ WHY THE ORIGINAL CHECK PASSED, and what changed so it cannot again.** `verify-notes-tier1.mjs` §3 waits for the panel before it types. That wait is exactly what a person does not do, and it is what made a data-writing bug look like a passing feature. The new rows assert BOTH halves every time — the list filtered to the expected note AND the underlying document byte-for-byte unchanged.
- **AND A MEASURED ADMISSION, recorded because it decides which row has teeth.** On a warm cache the race does not reproduce in this sandbox at all: against the broken build the timing rows stayed green at 55 ms between keystrokes **and** at full speed, because Playwright's key dispatch is slower than a React commit once the chunk is downloaded. So the two rows that actually catch it are the **deterministic** one — focus is put back in the note with the palette open, which is his symptom with the race taken out — and the **cold** one, which delays the palette's chunk in a fresh browser context so the gap is a real network round trip.
- Sandbox: `ui-audit/verify-notes-tier1.mjs` §10–§12 (15 new rows). **Mutation-proven: reverting the gate, the `select()` removal and the focus restore turns 7 rows red**, including the deterministic focus row and all three cold-chunk rows — and the mutated build reproduces the owner's report exactly (`Quadvest` in the document, list unfiltered). Full suite green, lint 0 errors, build green.

- **⛔ RESTORING CREATES A NEW VERSION. IT NEVER DESTROYS HISTORY.** The state being left is snapshotted and PINNED first, so restoring the wrong version is itself undoable by restoring the one taken a second earlier. The rule is a pure function (`planRestore`) whose unit test asserts the plan contains **no delete of any kind** — the property, stated, rather than a comment claiming it.
- **⛔ AND IT GOES THROUGH THE OPEN EDITOR, NOT ROUND THE BACK OF IT.** Writing the restored JSON straight to storage while an editor holds the old document is a silent-loss bug by construction: the editor's own unmount flush writes its stale copy back over the restore a moment later. Handed to the editor it is one ordinary transaction — undoable, saved by the one save path, visible immediately.
- **RETENTION IS DENSER RECENT, COARSER AS IT AGES** — everything inside the last hour, hourly for a day, daily for a month — and **the newest row is pinned unconditionally**, because a history whose current row can be swept is a history that can be empty at the exact moment you need it. Pure, so every tier boundary is a test.
- **⛔ SNAPSHOTS LIVE IN INDEXEDDB, NEVER LOCALSTORAGE (TIER-BY-REBUILDABILITY).** The small tier was measured at ~78% of a hard ~5 MB cap on the owner's own browser with real saved plans in it; a note's typing history is bulky and bursty and would crowd irreplaceable work out of exactly the store that must never fill.
- **A BUG THE HARNESS CAUGHT, AND IT IS THIS FILE'S OWN CLEANUP-ORDER TRAP ONE LAYER ALONG.** The unmount snapshot read `pendingRef`, which the SAVE flush empties — and the flush's cleanup is registered earlier, so it runs first. The snapshot found null every time and took no version at all, silently, because "no versions yet" is also what an untouched page looks like. It reads its own ref now, which nothing clears.
- **STATED LIMIT, filed as its own item rather than left implied: history is DEVICE-LOCAL — see B298759.**

### B298400 — THE NUMBER: Harris County's whole NFHL floodplain bakes to 5.96 MiB, 23.8% of the Cloudflare Pages per-file cap `[Site Planner / GIS]` (task) #gis #floodplain #perf #infra  *(filed 2026-08-09 from the owner chat block "Planyr — floodplain performance, Phase 1", item NEW-1 — an explicit MEASUREMENT SPIKE whose stated primary deliverable is "a real measured byte count, not a feature". Minted **B298400** from this branch's reserved block B298400–B298415, against freshly-fetched origin/main f797f8c. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `PMTiles`, `tippecanoe`, `NFHL`, `S_FLD_HAZ_AR`, `flood tile`, `bake`, `hazards.fema.gov`, `build-*.mjs`: `scripts/build-admin-boundaries.mjs` and `build-county-polygons.mjs` are the closest prior art — both bake an agency layer into a committed `public/` asset for exactly this reason — but neither touches FEMA and neither emits tiles. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-09 — all six live-site counties built, byte-verified, and committed. Harris (the worst case) is 5.96 MiB. NO fallback was needed and none was applied.**
- Verify: sandbox — the script ran HERE against the live FEMA service, and `test/floodTiles.test.js` reads the COMMITTED archives back and asserts the shipped bytes honour the rule.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-09 from chat; shipped the same session.
- **⛔ THE DELIVERABLE, FIRST, because it is the point of the item.** Measured against the **25 MiB Cloudflare Pages free per-file cap**:

  | county | archive | bytes | MiB | % of cap | polygons kept | NFHL effective |
  |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
  | **harris** | `flood-tx-harris.pmtiles` | **6,246,238** | **5.96** | **23.8%** | 9,585 | 2019-11-15 |
  | chambers | `flood-tx-chambers.pmtiles` | 1,739,990 | 1.66 | 6.6% | 2,834 | 2018-01-19 |
  | fortbend | `flood-tx-fortbend.pmtiles` | 1,469,898 | 1.40 | 5.6% | 1,749 | 2021-01-29 |
  | co_larimer | `flood-co-larimer.pmtiles` | 900,748 | 0.86 | 3.4% | 2,788 | 2021-01-15 |
  | waller | `flood-tx-waller.pmtiles` | 719,659 | 0.69 | 2.7% | 1,510 | 2019-05-16 |
  | co_adams | `flood-co-adams.pmtiles` | 665,070 | 0.63 | 2.5% | 1,638 | 2021-12-02 |

  **Total 11.2 MiB across 7 files** (six archives + the manifest), against a 20,000-file deployment limit. **Harris is the worst case in the set and it clears the cap with 76% to spare, so NEITHER fallback the brief named — split by watershed, or drop to z12 — was needed, and neither was silently applied.** The script exits non-zero and prints both options rather than working around an oversize county.
- **THE SPIKE'S GATE WAS RESPECTED, AND THEN PASSED.** The brief said *"do not scale to all counties until Harris is measured."* Harris was built and measured FIRST (5.96 MiB), and only then were the other five built. **Larimer was the required non-Texas check and it passed unchanged** — same script, same code path, correct `08069C` study and `Jan 15, 2021` vintage.
- **WHAT THE SCRIPT DOES** (`scripts/build-flood-tiles.mjs`, `npm run build:floodtiles -- harris co_larimer` / `-- --all` / `--dry-run`). Pages NFHL layer 28 by `DFIRM_ID LIKE '<fips>%'`, projects to the four attributes the identify card reads, drops what FEMA paints nothing for, and pipes newline-delimited GeoJSON through **tippecanoe** to `-Z8 -z13`. It emits a sibling `public/flood/manifest.json` recording, per county: the NFHL effective date (newest FIRM panel) AND the oldest panel's, the DFIRM study ids, published/fetched/kept counts, what was dropped and why, the pyramid, the measured bytes, and the tippecanoe version. The manifest is **merged, not overwritten**, so a one-county rebuild cannot silently retire another archive's vintage.
- **⛔ THE DROP RULE RUNS THROUGH THE APP'S OWN CLASSIFIER, so the archive and the app cannot disagree.** `resolveFloodZone` (`floodZone.js`) decides keep/drop, not a substring test in the script. **Unshaded Zone X is dropped** — FEMA's own renderer paints nothing for it, so absence of a polygon means outside the mapped floodplain (Harris: 1,217 of 10,802 polygons, 11%). **Shaded Zone X is KEPT**, including the five subtypes beyond `0.2 PCT` that FEMA paints in the 0.2% class (`1 PCT DEPTH LESS THAN 1 FOOT` and `1 PCT DRAINAGE AREA LESS THAN 1 SQUARE MILE` alone are 54k polygons nationally) — a narrower test would have thrown away exactly the band that drives COH Ch.19, Fort Bend §9 and Waller §A(8). `STATIC_BFE`'s `-9999` sentinel becomes an honest absent value rather than riding into a tile to be printed as an elevation.
- **⛔ NOTHING IS EVER DROPPED FOR SIZE.** `--no-feature-limit --no-tile-size-limit` are deliberate and must stay: tippecanoe's defaults drop features out of dense tiles to stay under 500 KB, which for a regulatory flood map means a floodplain silently disappearing at one zoom in one place — the single worst thing this layer could do. Simplification below the max zoom stays on; that is generalisation of a shape, not removal of a feature, and it is what makes a tile a picture rather than a number. `--detect-shared-borders` keeps adjacent zones simplifying identically so no hairline gaps open between them.
- **⛔ ONE REAL BUG THE SPIKE FOUND, MEASURED RATHER THAN GUESSED: FEMA 500s ON A BIG RESPONSE, NOT ON A BAD REQUEST.** Harris rows 10,000–10,802 are large multi-ring polygons. Asking for all 802 in one page returns `HTTP 500` after ~10 s, **every time**, with a 636-byte error body. The IDENTICAL query at `resultRecordCount=400` returns 200 and **12.6 MB in 9.8 s**; 200 rows → 2.1 MB; 100 rows → 0.64 MB. So the constraint is response SIZE, and a fixed page size cannot work for a county whose polygon complexity varies by two orders of magnitude. **The first version of this script retried the same oversize page four times, which is the one strategy guaranteed to fail.** The fetch now HALVES its window on failure and grows it back on success, always retrying the SAME offset so no row can be skipped. Fort Bend needed it too, at offset 0.
- **⛔ AND ONE PAGING RULE THAT LOOKS LIKE TIDINESS AND IS NOT:** `orderByFields=OBJECTID`. `resultOffset` paging over an unordered result set is undefined — the service may return a row twice and skip another, and the totals still look plausible. The fetch also dedupes by OBJECTID and reports any short count loudly rather than shipping a quietly incomplete archive.
- **⛔ THE COST WORTH FLAGGING, since nobody asked me to weigh it: 11.2 MiB of BINARY now lives in git history, and every NFHL refresh adds another ~11 MiB, permanently.** That is the real price of `public/`-as-delivery, and it is the thing to revisit before this scales past a handful of counties (a build-time fetch, or an out-of-band asset store, would trade it for a build dependency). It is cheap at this size and it does not shrink.
- **GUARD.** `test/floodTiles.test.js` reads the COMMITTED archives with the real PMTiles reader and asserts, per county: the file exists and matches its recorded size · it fits the 25 MiB cap · it carries a real NFHL effective date · the pyramid is z8–z13 and the tile type is MVT · every attribute is one of the declared four. Plus a spread of 16 real z13 tiles across Harris in which **no dropped variant and no `-9999` sentinel may appear**, with a floor on how many polygons were actually inspected so an empty sample cannot pass as a clean one.

### B298402 — A baked tileset has a vintage, so the panel says which edition of the NFHL it is drawing `[Site Planner / GIS]` (feature) #gis #floodplain #ui #site-planner  *(filed 2026-08-09 from the owner chat block "Planyr — floodplain performance, Phase 1", item NEW-3. Minted **B298402** from this branch's reserved block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `vintage`, `as of`, `effective date`, `EFF_DATE`, `data age`, `B75`, `B1093`, `layerVintage`: **B75** surfaces a PROXY-CACHE age ("flood data 16h ago") — that is how stale our COPY of a live answer is, a different fact from which EDITION of the map is being drawn; `layers.layerVintage` is the per-source registry note and does not read a manifest. **B1093** is the honest-empty-state rule this item follows rather than duplicates. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-09 — the `REGULATORY` tier heading reads `· NFHL as of Nov 15, 2019` whenever tiles are the source, and says so out loud when the date cannot be read.**
- Verify: sandbox — driven headless HERE (`verify-flood-tiles.mjs` arm D, both directions); no live blocker applies to the stamp itself. The flag it rides behind is B298401's, and that is V96960's.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-09 from chat; shipped the same session.
- **WHY IT EXISTS.** A LIVE layer needs no vintage — whatever it draws is whatever FEMA is serving this second. The moment the picture comes out of a file we built, *"when was this true?"* becomes a question the panel has to be able to answer. **A fast map that is quietly six months stale is worse than a slow one that is right, because nothing about it looks wrong.**
- **WHERE IT RENDERS, and why there.** As a chip on the `REGULATORY` tier heading the FEMA row already sits under — **PANEL-BREVITY rule 3, a named state rather than a sentence explaining the state.** It therefore costs the default view **zero visible lines** (measured: `node ui-audit/panel-copy-budget.mjs --check` green before and after, every region within budget), and nothing had to be removed to pay for it. It is shown ONLY when tiles are the source; a live layer's vintage is "now" and stamping it would be noise.
- **⛔ IT CANNOT DISAPPEAR — that is the whole design.** `floodVintageStamp` returns `{ text, known, date }` and never null: a missing manifest, a malformed one, a county with no row, an empty date, or a date that is not `YYYY-MM-DD` all produce **"NFHL vintage unknown — this county's tiles carry no effective date"** in the warn colour. Omitting the line on a failed fetch is exactly the silent-absence failure B1093 exists to prevent, and the test asserts all eight failure shapes produce a non-empty "unknown".
- **THE DATE IS SPELLED, NOT SLASHED.** `Nov 15, 2019`, not `11/15/2019` — a FIRM effective date is a legal fact, and a slashed numeric date reads as a US date to half the world and a day-first date to the other half. The county key is the SITE's own (the same one the archive is picked with), so the panel can never stamp one county's date over another county's map.
- **GUARD.** `test/floodTiles.test.js` — the stamp read out of the REAL committed manifest, every unknown-shape, the mixed-case county key (B298403), and the month-name formatting. Headless: `verify-flood-tiles.mjs` asserts the chip is on screen with tiles AND absent with the flag off.

### B298403 — `sites.county` was case-sensitive: two production plans spelled `Harris` and silently resolved no county sources at all `[Site Planner / Persistence]` (bug) #persistence #gis #site-planner #sync  *(filed 2026-08-09 from the owner chat block "Planyr — floodplain performance, Phase 1", item NEW-4. Minted **B298403** from this branch's reserved block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `county`, `countyKey`, `COUNTIES_MAP`, `countyKeyForName`, `case-sensitive`, `normalize`, `B1091`, `B209502`, `B209503`: **B1091** fixed a DIFFERENT county-key mismatch — the panel's `fortbend` vs an agency's `Fort Bend` — and its `floodGroup.countyKey` is a DISPLAY-NAME slug that strips non-letters, which would turn `co_larimer` into `colarimer`; it is not this and must not be reused for this. **B209502/B209503** are the point-in-polygon county answer and the Austin-county alias — neither touches the stored routing key. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-08-09 — normalised at every read and every write, the two production rows migrated, and a server-side trigger so the class cannot come back.**
- Verify: sandbox — unit-tested here, and the production migration was applied and re-queried in the same session (40 `harris`, 0 `Harris`).
- Origin: filed 2026-08-09 from chat; shipped the same session.
- **THE REPRO, CONFIRMED AGAINST PRODUCTION.** `select county, count(*) from public.sites group by 1` returned **38 `harris` and 2 `Harris`** (capital H, last written 2026-07-04) — and both the `county` COLUMN and the serialized model's `data->>'county'` carried the capital. `county` is used as an OBJECT KEY throughout (`COUNTIES_MAP[county]`, `COUNTY_DISTRICT[county]`, `defaultJurForCounty(county)`, `statewideFallbackFor(county)`, and now the baked-flood-tile archive pick), so those two plans missed every one of them.
- **⛔ WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE, WHICH IS THE WORST PART.** A missing object key is `undefined`, not a throw — and **every one of those call sites has a `|| fallback`**, so the miss rendered as a confident wrong answer. `defaultJurForCounty("Harris")` returned `"generic"` instead of `"coh"`, i.e. those two Harris plans were quietly using generic easement rules instead of City of Houston's. No banner, no dot, no telemetry. This is precisely the LOUD-FAILURE class.
- **⛔ THE FIX IS AT THE MAPS, NOT AT THE CALL SITES, and that is deliberate.** Patching call sites one at a time is HOW this class existed: `defaultFloodJurForCounty` already lower-cased and `defaultJurForCounty`, in a sibling module, did not. So `shared/gis/countyKeys.js` wraps the county-keyed config maps themselves (`COUNTIES`, `COUNTIES_MAP`, `JURISDICTION_LAYERS`, the two statewide county-name tables, `SNAPSHOT_COUNTIES`) in a normalising accessor — **no lookup can miss, including one written next year by someone who never reads this item.** `Object.keys` / `entries` / `in` all behave exactly as before; only a key absent under its literal spelling but present under its normalised one changes.
- **⛔ WHITESPACE IS REMOVED, NOT TURNED INTO AN UNDERSCORE, and that is a decision about THIS vocabulary.** The underscore in a routing key is a STATE PREFIX separator (`co_larimer`), never a word separator — this app keys the two-word counties `fortbend` and `sanjacinto`, run together. So `"Fort Bend"` normalises to `fortbend`; mapping the space to `_` would produce `fort_bend`, a key that exists nowhere, and would silently reintroduce the exact miss being closed. (The first version of the normaliser did that, and the test caught it.)
- **THE WRITE SIDE TOO, at three gates.** `createSiteModel` (the funnel every record passes through — a localStorage load, a cloud row, an import, every save-merge) · `cloudSync.siteRowFor` (the last gate before the `county` column, for a header-only path that never round-trips the model) · and a **server-side `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE` trigger**, so an import, a hand-edited row, a client that predates this fix, or a psql session cannot recreate it.
- **THE MIGRATION, APPLIED.** `db/sites_county_normalize.sql` — an immutable `public.norm_county_key(text)` mirroring the JS, the two rows fixed in **both** the column and the jsonb blob (normalising the column alone would leave the model still holding `Harris` on the next open, which is the lookup that was failing), and the trigger. **It is a TRIGGER, not a CHECK constraint, on purpose:** a CHECK would REJECT a mixed-case write, turning a silent wrong answer into a hard save failure for the user; normalising is the behaviour actually wanted, because the key means the same thing either way. **`updated_at` is deliberately NOT bumped even on the rows it changes** — it is the CAS input the optimistic-concurrency layer compares against, and a housekeeping rewrite that moved it would hand every open tab a spurious "changed in another session" conflict on a field the user never touched. Re-queried after applying: **40 `harris`, 0 `Harris`.**
- **A NICE SIDE-EFFECT WORTH RECORDING:** the repo's own e2e fixture `e2e/fixtures/sites/dense-testfit.fixture.json` carried `"county": "Harris"` and regenerated to `"harris"` on the next `node scripts/build-fixtures.mjs`. The bug was in the test corpus too.
- **GUARD.** `test/countyKeys.test.js` (36) — the normaliser, the map/set wrappers, and the brief's own acceptance test (*"a mixed-case county key still resolves its source set"*) asserted against the **REAL config maps**, not a fixture, because the bug was never in a normaliser — it was in the maps not using one. Both write gates are pinned by value.

### B304178 — Browser-driving rule: a synthetic Delete/Backspace does not delete, and one DOM read is not a check `[Infra / Testing]` (task) #infra #testing #selection  *(arrived 2026-08-09 as provisional NEW-3 in an owner chat block, after the second cleanup round it caused on his live plans. `[x]` **✅ DONE (sandbox — the claim is re-measured live by its own harness, which ran green here).**
- Verify: sandbox — `ui-audit/verify-delete-drive.mjs` drives the real app and proves both halves
- Origin: owner chat block, 2026-08-09
- **THE COST.** Two cleanup rounds on the owner's LIVE plans — the stray Bain easement (2026-08-08) and the three Silvestri markups (V27088, 2026-08-09). Both times the harness "deleted" the object, **reported success, and the object was still on his plan**, so a human had to finish it by hand.
- **THE MECHANISM, MEASURED not reasoned** (build 7307342, one selected building, element count before → after). The planner's key handler is bound to **`window`**, and `new KeyboardEvent(…)` defaults **`bubbles: false`** — a real key event never does — so a synthetic event on `document` / `document.body` never reaches it: `document` **1 → 1 ✗** · `document.body` **1 → 1 ✗** · `window` (the listener's own target) **1 → 0 ✓** · any of the three with `bubbles: true` **1 → 0 ✓** · `page.keyboard.press("Delete")` **1 → 0 ✓**. So it is NOT that the app rejects untrusted events — it never checks `isTrusted`. **One missing option, failing in total silence.**
- **TWO MORE GATES SWALLOW THE KEY BY DESIGN**, so a driver can do everything right and still no-op: a **FOCUSED FIELD** (the typing guard — correct product behaviour, invisible to a driver that did not blur) and an **INACTIVE PLANNER** (`if (!active) return`).
- **THE RE-READ HALF, which the item names.** The DOM read races the re-render, which is exactly how a pass was reported for an object still present. `deleteFeatureUntilGone` (`ui-audit/lib/deleteFeature.mjs`) escalates **key → Properties panel → context menu**, **polls until the feature is genuinely ABSENT between every attempt**, and **THROWS rather than reporting a pass it did not earn**; `deleteFeaturesAndConfirm` reloads and re-reads, because a removal that never reached storage comes back.
- **MACHINE-ENFORCED, and it cannot rot into folklore.** `test/deleteDrive.test.js` (12) pins the verdict table — including the state both live cleanups were in, which must be a LOUD failure — and **sweeps `ui-audit/` + `e2e/` for the banned shape**, mutation-checked both ways. `ui-audit/verify-delete-drive.mjs` is the **positive control**: it re-drives the banned shape against the real app every run and **fails if it ever starts working**, so the day the key wiring changes the rule says so instead of going quietly stale. Ran green here: three synthetic dispatches left the feature exactly where it was; the documented path removed it on the first attempt and the census moved 1 → 0.
- **Named rule added to `CLAUDE.md` beside FOREGROUND-OR-VOID: SYNTHETIC-KEYS-DONT-EDIT.** (COUNT-EVERY-KIND, B304177's rule, sits with it.)

- **⛔ THE FINGERPRINT HAS TO BE STRUCTURAL, and that is why the class hid.** Every instance returns a FRESH object holding an IDENTICAL answer, so `Object.is` — all React's memo does — says "changed" on 100% of them. A reference compare finds nothing, forever.
- **⛔ HALF THE CLASS IS NOT IN A MEMO AT ALL**, which is why exported library functions are instrumented too: the pond label fit, instance two, is a plain function called from the render body. No dispatcher patch could ever have seen it.

Four verdicts: `once` ✅ · `redundant` (missing memo) · `view-churned` (mis-keyed memo — the class the owner named) · `productive` (the answer genuinely moved — NOT a violation).

### B265537 — `event:perf`'s `t` is WALL SECONDS, not interacting time: the fifth false lead, refuted before it was chased `[Platform / Infra]` (bug) #perf #infra #testing  *(filed 2026-08-08 from the owner chat block, ITEM 1's data note, verbatim: "CONFIRM THE SEMANTICS OF t before treating it as one, because misreading a counter is how this program has produced four false findings." He was right to hedge. Minted **B265537** from this branch's block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched `perfInstrument`, `secondsSinceLoad`, `longtask`, `cumulative`, `B1121`, `B1435`, `B255200`: no prior item touches the row's SHAPE. Net-new.)*
`[ ]` **✅ CONFIRMED AND REFUTED — the lead dissolves, and the row now carries deltas so it cannot be misread again.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-08-08 from chat
- **THE SEMANTICS, settled two independent ways.** `t: num(sample.secondsSinceLoad)` where `secondsSinceLoad = (performance.now() − t0) / 1000` — **wall-clock SECONDS since the instrument installed.** Not milliseconds, and not interacting time (that counter exists, but it belongs to the RECORDER, which reports it as `activeMs`). Checked against his own rows: 21:52:38Z carried `t 9955` and 03:01:00Z carried `t 28457`; the difference is **18,502**, and the wall-clock gap is **18,502 seconds exactly**.
- **⛔ SO THE LEAD IS REFUTED.** The reported pair — *"t advanced only 237 ms while long tasks rose by 19 and blocked time by 1,835 ms"* — is his 23:07:19 → 23:11:16 rows, and `t` advanced **237 SECONDS**, not milliseconds (the wall gap is 237 s to the second). 1,835 ms of blocking over 237 s is a **0.8% duty cycle** — ordinary, not work landing outside interaction. **This would have been the programme's fifth false finding**, and it was avoided only because the owner asked for the counter to be confirmed first.
- **THE FIX, so no reader has to difference the right pair.** Every row after the first now carries `dt` (seconds elapsed), `dlt` (blocked ms) and `dltn` (long tasks) **against the previous row from the same tab**, and `t` / `lt` / `ltn` / `ltx` are documented at the source as wall-seconds and cumulative-since-load (`ltx` a high-water mark). Guard: `test/capturePipe.test.js` pins the arithmetic on his real numbers, including the wall-clock reconciliation above.

### B265540 — A manual capture taken in a still moment arrived EMPTY and looked ordinary `[Platform / Infra]` (bug) #perf #infra #testing  *(found 2026-08-08 by B265536's own harness, `manual-cold` arm. Net-new.)*
`[ ]` **✅ SHIPPED.**
- Verify: sandbox
- **THE CASE.** The frame loop is gated on interaction by design (an idle tab's frame deltas measure the browser's throttling policy, not the app). So a manual press in a still moment — he notices a panel is stuck, he has not moved the pointer for five seconds — legitimately has NO frame track. That capture is still worth having: it carries the long tasks, the scene and the counter history. ### B265541 — The jankier the episode, the likelier the capture arrived with NO frames at all `[Platform / Infra]` (bug) #perf #infra #testing  *(found 2026-08-08 by B265536's harness on its FIRST real induced stall — one auto capture came back `note:"trimmed-hard"`, `framesKept:0`. Minted **B265541** from this branch's block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched `encodeCapture`, `shedFrames`, `trimmed-hard`, `CAPTURE_MAX_CHARS`, `B255200`: the encoder's own header already declared the intended rule this violated. Net-new.)*
`[ ]` **✅ SHIPPED — and it is the worst-aimed defect of the set.**
- Verify: sandbox
- **THE MECHANISM, and it is perverse.** A frame over 63 ms will not fit the packed track's one base-64 digit, so it is ALSO carried in `fx` as `[index, ms]` — about ten characters apiece. On a smooth capture almost nothing lands there; **on a genuine stall almost every frame does**, so 60 retained frames can cost ~660 characters on their own. The shed stopped dead at 60 and a row that still overran fell through to the bare last-resort row, which drops EVERY series — frame track included. **A capture of a bad moment is the only kind worth having, so the failure was aimed squarely at the data this programme exists to collect.**
- **THE FIX.** The floor is a ladder (60 → 30 → 16 → 8), and the other series are surrendered BEFORE the frames are — which is what the file's own comment already said should happen (*"frames go last because the frame track IS the episode"*): the counter and task floors were consuming the room the track needed. `framesKept` / `framesDropped` still state exactly what was lost, so a shorter episode can never read as a calmer one. The bare row remains reachable and still says so.

### B246531 — The backlog index silently dropped every RECURRENCE — the eleven items a session most needs to see `[Infra / Testing]` (bug) #infra #testing  *(found 2026-08-08 while filing B1121's third recurrence: the item was bumped to `(×3)`, the index was regenerated, and **B1121 did not appear in it** — nor had it ever. Minted **B246531** LATE via `--against-main` from this branch's reserved block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `BACKLOG_OPEN`, `build-backlog-index`, `index`, `drift`, `recurrence`, `B636`, `B638`: **B638** built the index and its tag-legend guard; **B636** defined the recurrence rule whose own notation this parser could not read. Neither noticed. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE — the `(×N)` marker is optional in the heading pattern, the count is carried into the row, and both directions are pinned by test.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: found 2026-08-08 in-session
- **THE DEFECT.** `parseBacklog`'s heading pattern was `/^###\s+(B\d+)\b\s*[—-]\s*(.*)$/` — the em-dash had to follow the id immediately. The recurrence rule (**B636**) mandates the opposite shape for a fix that did not stick: `### B1121 (×3) — …`. So every recurrence-marked heading failed to match and its item was **dropped from `BACKLOG_OPEN.md` silently**, because a dropped item is indistinguishable from an item that does not exist. `--check` stayed green throughout: the index was a faithful render of a parse that had already lost the rows.
- **⛔ WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SIZE.** `CLAUDE.md` tells every session to **grep `BACKLOG_OPEN.md` for the live open set** rather than read the 250 KB backlog — so this is the file a session actually looks at, and the bug **selected precisely for the items that matter most**: a `(×N)` means a fix has already failed at least once. **Eleven Open / ⏳ Verify items were missing**, among them **B1121 (×3)** — the oldest unexplained bug in the speed program, the one this very session was dispatched on, and the one `CLAUDE.md`'s own perf notes point at. Recovered counts: **140 → 143 open, 306 → 314 awaiting verification.**
- **The fix.** `(?:\(×(\d+)\))?` between the id and the dash, and the count is **carried into the row** (`| B1121 (×3) | …`) rather than merely no longer fatal — a reader scanning for what to pick up should see "this has already failed twice" without opening the backlog.
- **Tests.** `test/backlogIndex.test.js` gains two cases, asserted **from `BACKLOG.md` itself** rather than from a fixture, so they cannot rot into a green that tests nothing: every `### B# (×N) —` heading in the real file that the parser collects must appear in the real index **with its count**, and a plain heading must carry `recurrences: null` and render as the bare id. 4 cases green.

### B246528 — The half of the owner's sentence nobody had used: a reload is an ELIMINATOR, and it takes whole families of suspect off the table `[Infra / Testing]` (task) #infra #testing #perf #site-planner  *(filed 2026-08-08 from the owner chat block as provisional NEW-1 — "hunt the symptom fresh … enumerate candidates before measuring … measure each as a GROWTH CURVE over a long session, not as a before/after pair." Minted **B246528** LATE via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main` from this branch's own reserved block; the code, tests and commits keep their provisional `NEW-#` labels. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `growth`, `retention`, `long session`, `reload`, `accumulate`, `B1121`, `B1331`, `B1357`, `B1432`, `B1433`, `B1434`, `B1439`: **B1121** owns the SYMPTOM and stays Open (re-opened ×3 here); **B1357/B1432** measured interaction COUNT on frozen content; **B1433** measured the browser layer; **B1434** owns the do-not-ship-a-blind-fix rule this item obeys; **B1439** is the retired plan-switch artefact. **Not one of them ever reloaded the page.** Net-new instrument.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE — the instrument shipped, the run was taken, and the result is an HONEST NULL on the cost curve plus three findings that were not being looked for. Full report: `docs/PERF-SESSION-GROWTH.md`.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-08-08 from chat
- **THE IDEA, and it is the only genuinely new thing in this item.** The owner's report contains two facts and this program had used only one. *"cost rises with time in session"* is a DETECTOR. *"if I reload, it's immediately pretty quick"* is an **ELIMINATOR** — a reload destroys the document, the heap, the DOM, every listener, timer and in-memory cache, and destroys **none** of localStorage, IndexedDB, the HTTP cache or the V8 code cache. So **anything that survives a reload cannot be the mechanism**, however perfectly it correlates. That single inference takes the whole durable-storage family off the table — which is where a reasonable person starts, and where **TIER-BY-REBUILDABILITY** (B1427/B1429) had most recently pointed. The caveat is stated in the code rather than left to be rediscovered: a durable store is excluded as the cause of the SLOPE, never as a contributor to a CONSTANT cost, which is B1121 complaint (b).
- **A CURVE, NOT A PAIR — because a pair cannot be asked the question.** Two points fit a step and a line equally well. `classifyCurve` fits FLAT / STEP / SLOPE / SAWTOOTH, reports each model's residual, requires a 35% improvement over the constant null before preferring a richer model, and **refuses to name any shape for a series whose whole range fits inside the measured noise floor**. That refusal is the load-bearing branch: this program has already paid for four shapes fitted to noise.
- **THE ENUMERATION IS PRE-REGISTERED AND COMMITTED** (`GROWTH_CANDIDATES`, 22 candidates in six families), each with a PREDICTION about whether a reload zeroes it, made in advance and **scored afterwards** — so a contradicted prediction is visible rather than invisible. Four are **not observable from outside the app** and are recorded as open questions rather than dropped: `undoDepth`, `gisCacheEntries`, `pendingJournalOps`, `telemetryBuffer`. An unmeasured candidate is an open question, not an exonerated one.
- **Shipped:** `ui-audit/session-growth.mjs` (the driver, `npm run perf:growth`) + `ui-audit/lib/sessionGrowth.mjs` (the pure half: registry, fits, classifier, the reload eliminator, the two-axis admissibility, the attribution ceiling). **NO PRODUCT CODE CHANGED, deliberately** — see B1434's rule and the result below.
- **Tests.** `test/sessionGrowth.test.js` — 37 cases. Every shape asserted on a series whose true shape is known by construction, **including the two that must NOT be named** (noise, and a series too short to have a shape); every quadrant of the eliminator asserted individually; and the ceiling asserted from both directions — correlation PROMOTES an admissible candidate to SUSPECT and **never rescues a reload-excluded one**, tested with a candidate correlating at r = 1.00.

### B246530 — A plan-switch verdict that samples once cannot tell RETENTION from NOT-YET-SWEPT — and a forced collection does not settle it `[Infra / Testing]` (bug) #infra #testing #perf #site-planner  *(found 2026-08-08 by B246528's growth curve while re-taking B246529's readings — the re-take reported a leak and the curve contradicted it in the same session. Minted **B246530** LATE via `--against-main` from this branch's reserved block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `plan switch`, `detached`, `collectGarbage`, `conservative`, `retained`, `B1439`, `B221762`, `B1433`: **B1439** is the *harness handle* artefact, fixed and closed, and is a DIFFERENT defect in the same measurement — this one survives that fix; **B221762** owns the heap-walk instrument. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE — `planSwitchVerdict` takes a settle sample and gains two verdicts. A one-sample run can no longer produce the word RETAINED.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: found 2026-08-08 in-session
- **THE FALSE POSITIVE, measured.** Re-taken on two real plans, the plans axis reported **RETAINED — `retainedHeapMB +39.1%`, `rendererNodes +38.1%`** after one A→B→A round trip, read after **two forced `HeapProfiler.collectGarbage` calls**. `ui-audit/session-growth.mjs` sampled the same counters across four switch rounds of a long session and saw the identical spike each time — and saw it **gone one ordinary round of work later, every time**, settling BELOW where the session began (detached≈ 185 → 1245 → 203 → 1028 → 168 → 1199 → 168; renderer nodes at rest 2355 → 2230 → 2011 → 2082).
- **WHY THE FORCED COLLECTION DOES NOT HELP, which is the part that makes this a real trap rather than a sloppy read.** V8's **conservative stack scanning** pins objects still referenced from the frames on the stack when the collection runs, so the outgoing tree survives the purge and is collected a moment later. `docs/PERF-PLAN-SWITCH.md` §14 had already recorded exactly this effect — *"a forced purge drains 2,343 → 1, but both natural allocation pressure and a precise cache-neutral `gc({execution:'async'})` do not"* — and the single-sample verdict was built anyway. Collecting twice is not a second sample.
- **The fix:** `planSwitchVerdict({ a0, b, a1, a2 })`. **`RETAINED`** now requires the counter to be elevated at A₁ **and still elevated after a settle**; a spike that decays is **`TRANSIENT`** (*"a single sample here would have reported a leak"*); a spike with no settle sample is **`UNSETTLED`** — explicitly neither verdict, naming conservative stack scanning as the reason. The harness takes A₂ after a `--switch-settle` wait and prints A₂ and its delta **beside** A₁ rather than instead of it, so the transient and its decay are both visible.
- **⛔ THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the second one this family has produced.** B1439's was *"the instrument's own protocol handles are part of the measured heap."* This one is **"a counter read once, immediately, cannot distinguish a level from a transient — and the collector you called to make it a level does not make it one."** Both were found the same way: by an instrument that samples the same quantity more than once.
- **✅ RE-RUN WITH THE FIX, AND THE VERDICT FLIPS TO `TRANSIENT` WITH EVERY COUNTER COMING HOME.** Same two real plans, same regime: `rendererNodes` **A₀ 2190 → B 3784 → A₁ 3150 (+43.8%) → A₂ 2089 (−4.6%)** — transient. And **four of the six counters return to their EXACT starting value** after the settle: event listeners 1600 → 1600, document elements 1692 → 1692, canvas nodes 600 → 600, layout objects 1391 → 1391. `retainedHeapMB` lands at +0.8%. A plan switch on two real, unrelated, raster-bearing plans releases everything it took.
- **Also fixed in passing: the report header named the WRONG SCENE.** It hard-coded `SCENARIO_ID`, so a `--fixture` run printed *"scenario perf-reference-goose-creek"* over numbers taken on Bain and Sylvestri — which is how a real reading gets filed against the wrong plan, the exact defect B246529 exists to close.
- **Tests.** `test/sessionAxes.test.js` gains four cases including the exact measured numbers as a regression fixture — RETAINED requires the settle sample to agree · the real +39.1%/+38.1% spike with a decaying A₂ must read `TRANSIENT` · a one-sample spike must read `UNSETTLED` and never `RETAINED` · and a clean round trip still reads `RELEASED` with no settle sample, so the change costs nothing when nothing spiked. 34 cases green.
