### B1174 — Double-clicking a measurement's LABEL does nothing `[Site Planner / measure]` (bug) #site-planner #ui #markup #selection  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-2. **REGRESSION from #866.** Minted **B1174** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`, late per B779. Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `isDoubleTap`, `startMeasChip`, `measure`, `Properties`, `label chip`: **B1151** (#866) is the item that INTRODUCED the chip and whose own guard failed to catch this — it is Done and stays Done, since this is a distinct defect in what it shipped rather than the same fix not sticking; **B938** gave measurements a Properties menu; **B750** is the double-click-opens-Properties parity rule this restores. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30.** The label chip now opens Properties on a double-click, exactly as the geometry does — on every measure mode, not just the reported one.
- Verify: sandbox — driven end-to-end in a real browser, logged out, on BOTH an area and a length measurement (`e2e/measure-drag-props.spec.js`, 2 new cases, green).
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **THE REPORT.** Draw an area measurement, double-click its label chip: nothing. Double-clicking the geometry works.
- **AUDIT-FIRST — the diagnosis is CONFIRMED exactly as written.** `startMeasChip` was the only handler on the label chip and it never called `isDoubleTap` — it selected and armed a drag, nothing else. It did not even write `lastTapRef`, so the gesture was completely unarmed on that element. There is no id mismatch: `isDoubleTap` had 8 call sites and the chip was not one of them.
- **WHY IT IS A REGRESSION, and the mechanism worth keeping in mind.** #866 REPLACED the old label. The old one was a `pointerEvents="none"` `<text>` at the polygon centroid, and an area's grab layer is a transparent FILLED polygon covering the whole interior — so a double-click on the old label fell THROUGH to the fill and reached `startMoveMeasure`. #866 put a pointer-enabled chip on that same spot, painted AFTER the hit path so it wins the hit test (deliberately, so its own drag would not be swallowed — that ordering has its own assertion), with a handler that had no double-tap branch. Same click, now a dead end.
- **BOTH CASES FIXED, as instructed.** Line/polyline measurements were a PRE-EXISTING gap rather than a regression — their old label sat outside the stroke's hit band and very likely never worked — and one `chipNode` serves every mode, so the single branch covers all of them. Both are driven in the browser.
- **THE FIX, placed as diagnosed.** The double-tap branch sits after `if (!m) return;` and BEFORE the lock guard, because `startMoveMeasure` opens Properties for a locked measurement too and the two surfaces must agree. It keys on the bare `m.id`, so a press on the chip pairs with a press on the shape and vice versa. Returning early also skips the `pushHistory()` the chip press would otherwise push as a no-op undo frame.
- **THE GUARD — this is the point of the item, and it was widened rather than trusted.** `test/measureWiring.test.js` already asserted double-click-opens-Properties and stayed green through this regression, because it source-scraped `startMoveMeasure` ONLY. **B1151 recorded that guard as protection against exactly this class and it did not protect.** It now DISCOVERS the surfaces from the render — every `onPointerDown` bound inside the measurement block — instead of naming one, so a new surface shipped without the gesture goes red on arrival. The generalisation is structural, never a name list: a handler that selects a SUB-PART (it writes `setSelVtx({…})`) is a vertex grip, which is a handle on an already-selected object rather than a way to reach the object, and no vertex handler anywhere in the planner reconstructs the double-tap — that invariant is itself asserted, so the exclusion cannot quietly rot into an excuse.
- **THE WIDENED GUARD IMMEDIATELY FOUND A THIRD SURFACE** the report did not mention — `startMeasureVertex` — and classified it correctly rather than either failing spuriously or ignoring it. That is the behaviour the widening was for.
- Files: `src/workspaces/site-planner/SitePlanner.jsx` (`startMeasChip`), `test/measureWiring.test.js` (the widened guard, +9 cases), `e2e/measure-drag-props.spec.js` (2 new browser cases).

### B1176 — The pinch teardown was the one gesture-ending path that did not settle its pending frame `[Site Planner]` (bug) #site-planner #ui  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-4, found incidentally while auditing NEW-3. Minted **B1176**. Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `flushFrameJobs`, `pinch`, `cancelActiveMove`, `abortGesture`: **B1157** (#869) built the frame-coalescing and wired `onUp` + `abortGesture`; **B555** built the native-touch pinch; **B315** owns the cancel-reverts-to-pre-drag contract. Nothing owns the third teardown path. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30.** `onTouchStartPinch` now settles the coalesced frame before it tears the gesture down, like every other path.
- Verify: sandbox — the invariant is proven structurally across ALL teardown paths by a discovering guard (`test/renderBudgetMemos.test.js`); there is no user-visible behaviour change to live-verify, and no named `Blocker:` wall, so this is correctly not a `V###`.
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **⚠ THE REPORTED MECHANISM IS CORRECTED, not implemented as told.** The report was that a pending coalesced `geom` job can land AFTER `cancelActiveMove()` and re-apply the vertex the cancel just undid. **That cannot happen today**, and the two halves never meet: the three drags that schedule a `geom` job (`vertex` · `elVertex` · `measureVertex`) set NO `canceler`, and `cancelActiveMove` is `if (!d || !d.canceler) return false` — a no-op without one. The drags that DO carry a canceler (`move`, `groupMove`) write their geometry synchronously and schedule no frame job at all. So there is no revert for a job to land on top of, and no vertex is resurrected. Verified by reading every `drag.current` assignment, not inferred.
- **WHAT IS REAL, and why it still shipped.** The pinch tears down `drag.current` with a `geom` job still queued, so that job commits one unrequested geometry write on the NEXT animation frame — after the pinch has taken the gesture over, after the view was deliberately restored, and outside any React batch. The committed coordinate happens to match, so **today this is an ordering defect rather than a data-loss one, and the item says so rather than overclaiming.** It becomes a data-loss one the moment a vertex drag gains a canceler — which is a natural thing to add (Esc-mid-drag revert, the B315 treatment `move` already has) and would silently arm exactly the bug as reported. The invariant is cheap to hold now and expensive to rediscover later.
- **FLUSH vs DISCARD — decided explicitly, as asked, and on the corrected facts. FLUSH.** Two reasons. (1) Every other teardown flushes, and one contract beats two: a `discardFrameJobs()` would be a second, subtly different teardown rule, and paths diverging from each other is precisely how this one got missed. (2) Flushing is the SAFE direction under the latent case above — `cancelActiveMove` reverts by replaying a whole-layer snapshot rather than a delta, so commit-then-revert lands on exactly the state a discard would, while discard would ADDITIONALLY throw away jobs the canceler does not own (the coalesced `cursor` job; a `geom` job from a canceler-less drag), which is a real behaviour change with nothing asking for it.
- **THE GUARD IS DISCOVERING, for the same reason as B1174.** The existing assertion named `onUp` and `abortGesture`, which is why the third path was outside it. It now finds every arrow function in the component that calls `cancelActiveMove()` and requires each to flush first — a fourth teardown path added later is covered on arrival with no edit to the test.
- Files: `src/workspaces/site-planner/SitePlanner.jsx` (`onTouchStartPinch`), `test/renderBudgetMemos.test.js` (the discovering guard).

### B1177 — The mint gate proves the ids a PR FILES are unclaimed, and never checked the ids it ANNOUNCES `[Infra / CI]` (bug) #infra #testing  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-H — filed and fixed in response to the owner's instruction that "if the mint gate cannot catch a cross-PR B collision, that is a real gap and it should be filed". Minted **B1177**. Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `mint`, `check-mint`, `collision`, `idUniqueness`, `next-id`: **B779** (×2) built the gate and owns the FILED ids; **B780** extended `idUniqueness` across the live+archive pair. Neither looks at a commit subject, which is the only number a human reads. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30.** A commit subject may now only name backlog ids this branch actually filed; the gate goes red otherwise, naming the id and quoting the subject.
- Verify: sandbox — the pure verdict layer is unit-tested, including a case that REPRODUCES the #866 subject and goes red on it.
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **⚠ THE REPORTED COLLISION IS CORRECTED — the data is CLEAN and the gate DID its job.** The report was that PR #865 and PR #866 both claim B1144 / B1145 / B1146 and both claim V531, "a live ID collision on main". Audited against the merged files: **#865 filed B1144 / B1145 / B1146 + V532** (the bundle-gate trio) and **#866 filed B1151 / B1152 / B1153 + V534** (the measurement trio). There is **no duplicate heading anywhere**, `test/idUniqueness.test.js` is green, `next-id` reports no duplicate actives, and no stale `B1144`–`B1146` reference for the measurement work survives in code or tests. #866's ids were correctly renumbered before it merged — which is the gate working, not failing.
- **THE REAL GAP, which IS a gap and is what this item fixes.** Nobody updated #866's PR **title** or **body** after the renumber, and the squash-merge commit therefore carries the pre-renumber numbers. So `git log --oneline` and the GitHub PR list both show two commits announcing the same three numbers for entirely different features — which reads, correctly, as a collision, and is what the owner saw. #865 has the same defect on a smaller scale: its title says V531 while it filed V532. **Renumbering is exactly when this breaks**, because B779's late-bind rule moves the heading at the last possible moment and the subject was written first. Nothing checked the two against each other.
- **RECONCILED, and what was done about the existing commits:** nothing is edited in merged history — rewriting `main` to fix two subject lines would cost far more than it buys, and the FILES (the actual source of truth, and what every cross-reference resolves against) are already correct. The record instead lives here and on **V532** / **V534**, so anyone who later hits "#866 says B1144" has the answer. **What is fixed is the mechanism**, so it cannot recur.
- **THE FIX.** `scripts/check-mint.mjs` gains an ANNOUNCEMENT check beside the existing mint check: every `B###`/`V###` named in a commit subject this branch adds (measured from the merge base, so it covers exactly what this push adds) must exist as a `### B###` / `### V###` heading in this branch's backlog / verification files. Merge commits and `Nudge CI` commits announce nothing and are skipped. It checks the PROPERTY ("the number I announce is the number I filed"), never the ceremony — so a correct late renumber that also fixes the subject passes untouched, and a **recurrence passes too**, because a recurrence re-opens an existing heading and the heading is right there. It runs everywhere the gate already runs: the pre-push hook and the required build step.
- **WHY THE COMMIT SUBJECT IS THE RIGHT THING TO CHECK** even though the defect is visible in the PR title: GitHub pre-fills the PR title from the first commit subject and a squash merge writes the PR title back as the commit subject, so the two are the same string in practice — and the commit subject is the half that is checkable locally, before the push, with no API call.
- Files: `scripts/check-mint.mjs` (`idsNamedIn` + `announceVerdict` + the CLI failure path), `test/mintGuard.test.js` (+8 cases, one of them the #866 reproduction).
### B1164 — The mint gate's pre-push hook now installs itself; a fresh container had no local gate `[repo / tooling · workflow]` (bug) #infra  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-1. Minted **B1164** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`, late, as the last step before push. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done for `hooksPath`, `pre-push`, `hooks:install`, `githooks`, `prepare`, `postinstall` and the whole mint family B755 / B779 / B780 / B896 / B898 / B1140: B779×2 shipped the gate itself and its logic is correct — this is purely REACHABILITY, a follow-on, not a recurrence. Nothing else owns hook installation. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30 — `Verify: sandbox`, and the sandbox proof is a genuinely fresh clone with a real rejected push, not an assertion.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat (NEW-1).

**The defect, in one line: `.git/hooks` is not cloned and `npm run hooks:install` was a manual step nobody
runs.** So in a fresh dispatch container — which is EVERY container — `.githooks/pre-push` never fired. The
required CI step still blocked a bad merge, so `main` was never at risk; what was missing was the fast local
failure that saves a whole build cycle. Same defect class as the item it follows: **a protection present in
principle and absent in practice.**

**The fix — `scripts/install-hooks.mjs`, wired to npm's `prepare` lifecycle** (`npm install` and `npm ci`
both run it; `npm run hooks:install` still works and now calls the same script). Installation becomes a
property of installing dependencies rather than of somebody remembering. Each of the item's five
requirements is a `describe` block in `test/installHooks.test.js` (23 cases, real git, real repos in a temp
dir — a mocked `git config` would prove nothing about whether a push runs the hook):
- **(a) FRESH CLONE, no prior state** — sets `core.hooksPath` to the committed `.githooks/`, and **chmods
  the hook executable**, because an installed-but-unrunnable hook is precisely the silent no-op this exists
  to kill.
- **(b) IDEMPOTENT** — a second run reports `already` and writes nothing. An ABSOLUTE spelling of the same
  directory is recognised as the same wiring, not mistaken for someone else's config.
- **(c) NEVER SILENTLY NO-OPS** (the B898 LOUD-FAILURE rule) — five distinct un-armed verdicts, each with
  its own named block on stderr saying what is lost: `foreign` · `not-a-repo` · `git-unusable` ·
  `missing-hooks` · `failed`. The write is **read back** afterwards, so a `git config` that "succeeded" but
  did not take is reported as the failure it is. `missing-hooks` is checked FIRST: wiring `core.hooksPath`
  at an empty directory is the perfect silent no-op — git is happy, the config looks right, no hook runs.
- **(d) NEVER CLOBBERS a deliberate `core.hooksPath`** — a foreign value is left exactly as it was, named
  along with the config SCOPE it came from, with the one command to opt in. Only an explicit
  `npm run hooks:install -- --force` replaces it; nothing automatic takes that branch.
- **(e) THE CI REQUIRED STEP IS UNTOUCHED** — this adds fast local feedback, it does NOT become the
  guarantee. A test asserts the workflow still runs `node scripts/check-mint.mjs --ci`. Which is also why
  the installer **never fails `npm install`** (always exit 0; `--check` is the strict, write-nothing mode
  used by tests): a convenience installer that wedges `npm ci` would take the build down over a nicety.

**One correction found while proving it, kept as a test:** with `.git/config` unusable, git answers the
work-tree question with an ERROR rather than "false", and the first cut reported that as "not a git repo" —
which would send someone hunting the wrong problem. There is now a separate `git-unusable` verdict carrying
git's own words verbatim.

**The verification the item asked for, run end to end in a genuinely fresh clone** (a scratch bare remote
seeded from `origin/main` at `3e2370b`, then `git clone` → `npm ci`, nothing else):
- `core.hooksPath` **empty** before `npm ci` (and `.git/hooks` holding only git's samples — the starting
  state of every container), **`.githooks`** after it, from `prepare`, with the receipt line in npm's output.
- A real `git push` of a branch minting an already-claimed id was **REJECTED BY THE HOOK, locally, before
  any CI**: `⛔ MINT GATE FAILED … B1150 is at or below the claimed high-water mark B1163 — minted against a
  stale view … → renumber this branch's new B# ids starting at B1164`, **push exit 1, nothing left the
  machine.** Renumbering to the id it named and pushing again: `✅ Mint gate: B1164 is unclaimed…`, exit 0.
  **This is the first time the gate has ever stopped a real push** — see B1165 for why that is no longer
  something the field has to discover.
- Re-running the installer: no-op. A foreign `core.hooksPath`: reported, not clobbered, still `my-own-hooks`
  afterwards. A broken git: loud, and exit 0 so `npm install` survives.
- Suite green: **6,688 tests / 393 files**, lint 0 errors, build green.

### B1165 — Prove the mint gate BLOCKS: the rejection path is now a permanent CI self-test against real git refs `[repo / tooling · workflow]` (task) #infra  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-2. Minted **B1165** the same way, late. DEDUPE-FIRST — extends B779×2 / V531 and its `test/mintGuard.test.js`; builds on B780's uniqueness guard and B898's loud-failure rule. The gate's LOGIC is sound and is not being re-fixed, so this is not a recurrence.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30 — `Verify: sandbox`, proven RED-then-GREEN.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat (NEW-2).

**The gap: the gate had been exercised live exactly ONCE — on PR #864's own push — and that item was a
recurrence, so it minted nothing and had nothing to block.** `mintGuard.test.js` unit-tests the verdict and
`nextId.test.js` covers the git reader's edge cases, but the COMPOSED path (fetch → peer mirror → merge base
→ "added ids" → verdict → exit code) had never run against a genuine collision, and V531 parked the question
as "watch the field". This area has now failed twice after being declared fixed. **Waiting for an organic
collision to discover whether the collision-catcher works is the wrong verification strategy.**

**AUDIT FIRST, as the item required.** Read what already existed and added only the genuinely missing layer:
`mintGuard.test.js` is PURE (no git, no clock, no network) and pins the verdict table; `nextId.test.js` pins
`readRefFile`/ENOBUFS/bad-ref behaviour against this repo. Neither is duplicated. The missing layer is the
**end-to-end path against real refs**, which is what shipped.

**`test/mintGateE2E.test.js` — 11 cases, real git, real refs, and still hermetic.** "The remote" is a bare
repo in a temp dir and every fetch is over the local filesystem, so it runs inside the ordinary required
build with no network and no dependence on this repo's own branch state. The fixture is a real race: a base
main at B100/V50, a PEER branch that pushes B103/V53 and never merges, and then main moving on to B102/V52 —
so work branches fork from the base and genuinely cannot see either. `check-mint.mjs` gained a `--repo=<path>`
flag whose only caller is this test, so the assertions drive the REAL CLI, not a re-implementation:
- **(a) taken on `origin/main`** (main merged the number mid-flight — the B1140 case, caught via the merge
  base) → rejected, exit **1**, names `origin/main`, and the id it tells you to move to steps over the
  unmerged peer as well as main.
- **(b) taken on an IN-FLIGHT PEER BRANCH** — the window B779's first pass declared impossible and this fix
  newly covers → rejected, exit **1**, **names the peer branch**, and both id families are checked, not just B.
- **below the claimed high-water mark** (free today, minted against a view that is already gone) → rejected
  with its own distinct wording, because it reads differently to a human than "taken".
- **(c) a clean mint** above main and above every peer → allowed, exit **0**. A deliberate GAP is allowed too
  (B1140 established gaps are free; a gate demanding max+1 would have rejected the fix that broke that loop).
- **(d) a DEDUPE-FIRST RECURRENCE** — a heading moving from the archive back to the live file → `added` is
  empty, allowed, exit **0**, untouched. So the correct response to a repeat report never meets gate friction.
- **RESILIENCE:** a dead remote and a missing `origin/main` are UNVERIFIABLE, not a verdict — exit **2**
  locally, exit **0 with the loud `⚠ MINT GATE UNVERIFIED … UNGUARDED` warning under `--ci`**. A guard that
  becomes an outage is worse than the collision it prevents. A stale ref refuses rather than grading against
  a week-old view. And the gate leaves the clone byte-identical: HEAD, branch, shallow state and merge base
  all unchanged after a run.

**RED-then-GREEN, the discipline used throughout this area.** With `mintVerdict` deliberately neutered to
always return `ok`, the suite goes RED — 7 failures, the three blocking cases in this file plus the four in
`mintGuard.test.js` — and every allow-case stays green, so the test discriminates rejection from noise
rather than merely passing. Restored: 29/29 green.

**Cost:** ~5 s inside `npm test` (which runs ~65 s), no new dependency, no manual step, no network.

**V531 RE-SCOPED, not closed by assertion.** Three of its six strands are now proven on every build and are
struck from the entry with the reason: **(a) it catches a real one** (all three rejection shapes, red-then-
green), **(e) `--ci` draws the line in the right place** (the infrastructure split), **(f) the backstop is
undisturbed** (`idUniqueness` + the B780 cross-file guard run untouched in the same suite). Three remain, and
they remain because no self-test can reach them: **(b) no false red at REAL scale** — the self-test proves
the verdict against a handful of synthetic branches; only the field proves it against ~500 real ones with
their churn; **(c) the peer fetch stays affordable** as the branch count grows; **(d) the refusal is
actionable, not annoying** — pure ergonomics, observable only in how other sessions actually respond.

### B1159 — Five provably-safe memos in the SitePlanner render body (and four deliberately NOT memoised) `[Site Planner]` (task) #site-planner #perf  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-4. Minted **B1159** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`, late. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done for `memo`, `useMemo`, `render body`, `pondContours`, `criteriaFor`, and the perf family B1040/B1042/B1063/B1064/B1126/B1146: B1064 is code-splitting, B1126 is computed-but-never-rendered, B1158 is the panel gate. Nothing owns per-render recomputation of these specific values. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30 — `Verify: sandbox`, and the proof is a unit suite that pins each memo's input set, not a claim.** Build green, 6,562 tests green, lint 0 errors, bundle budgets within ceiling.
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat (NEW-4).

**A CORRECTION carried onto the record, because the dispatch that raised it corrected itself.** An earlier
brief said the drainage/detention engines are NONE memoised. **That is wrong.** Several already carry
module-level LRU memos — `lib/pondGeom.js`'s `_detMemo` (DET_MEMO_MAX 32), `_bandMemo`, `_excMemo`, and
`SitePlanner.jsx`'s `MIT_MEMO_MAX` guarding `_mitMemo` and `_pondFactsMemo` — and five `useMemo`s already key
correctly on hand-built signature strings (`gsSig`, `wedgeMitSig`, `pondConflictsSig`, `balancerSig`,
`drainSigNow`). What IS true is that 52 of 118 call sites across those modules run on every render. The
genuinely-unmemoised hot set is smaller and more actionable than the original claim, and that is what shipped.

**The five, each with a provably complete and enumerable input set:**
- **(a) `markupsZ`** was a fresh array identity every render, so the `useMemo` on the very next line
  (`drawMarkupsZ`) could **never** hit and `cullToView` re-scanned the whole markup layer on every frame of
  an unrelated drag. Memoised in name only. Now keyed on `[markups]` — the raw state value. One line.
- **(b) `drawEls`** was copied and sorted **twice per render** to split the same array at one z threshold.
  One memo over `[drawEls]` returning `{ below, above }`. Order within each half is unchanged (one stable
  sort over the whole set, then partitioned).
- **(c) `overlappingParcelPairs(parcels)` + `dissolvedParcelSqft(parcels, pairs)`** — both pure, both take
  `parcels` and nothing else, both O(n²) with ear-clip triangulation and Sutherland–Hodgman per pair and no
  memo anywhere in `lib/polyClip.js`. Keyed on `[parcels]`. This is also the single biggest contributor to
  B1157's vertex-drag cost.
- **(d) `criteriaFor(critJurKey, { overrides: criteriaOverrides })`** was called **11×** per render with
  byte-identical arguments — each `{ overrides: … }` literal being a fresh allocation of its own — and
  `lib/detentionCriteria.js` rebuilds a ~30-field object with nested provenance carriers each time. One memo
  on `[critJurKey, criteriaOverrides]`; a guard asserts exactly one `criteriaFor(critJurKey` survives.
- **(e) `pondContours`** had no memo, unlike every one of its neighbours in the same file — and it is the most
  expensive of them: `maxInwardOffset` alone is a 28-iteration binary search whose EVERY iteration runs a full
  `ClipperOffset.execute` with round joins, plus one `offsetInward` per contour level. Roughly **38 clipper
  runs per pond, per render**, worst exactly when you are zoomed in working on ponds. Given a module-level LRU
  keyed the way `detentionStorage` already keys itself in the same file. `opts` is accepted for call-site
  symmetry but never read, so `(ring, det)` is the whole input set — asserted by a test that changes each of
  depth / freeboard / slope / contourInterval / tobElev / the ring and requires a fresh result for each.

**Two de-duplications alongside them:**
- **`DET_MEMO_MAX` 32 → 128, with the reason.** Each pond generates roughly three distinct signatures per
  render (`pondSplitFor`, the `pondLedgerEntries` pass, and the map label loop each ask at a different
  depth/freeboard), so 32 held barely ten ponds and a real multi-pond plan evicted entries it was about to ask
  for again — the classic thrash where a cache costs and never pays. 128 covers ~40 ponds with headroom;
  entries are five-number objects, so the memory is noise. A test walks 40 rings and requires every one to
  still be resolvable.
- **`pondSplitOf`** reads a pond's split off the ledger pass that already computed it, instead of re-deriving
  it at three further sites. Pure de-duplication, no new dependency surface, and it falls back to a direct
  derivation for anything not in that pass (a probe element built as `{ ...el, det }`, or a pond that arrived
  after it) — so it can only ever save work, never change an answer.

**The four that were audited and REJECTED, and are asserted to STAY un-memoised.** A missed dependency over
flood/detention inputs produces a **stale engineering number**, which is worse than a slow correct one — so
this is written into the test suite rather than into a comment that rots:
- **`detReq` / `computeRequiredDetention`** — its input set includes `coDetention`, a closure over a lazily
  imported chunk, so the dep set is not enumerable; and it is arithmetic over a rules table, not geometry, so
  the payoff is near zero.
- **`pondLedgerEntries`**, **`pondBermScreen`**, **`fmEvalAtWse`** — same class. Each wants its own diff and a
  numeric regression test, not a line in a batch.

**Tests.** `test/renderBudgetMemos.test.js` (new, 39 assertions) pins each memo's exact dependency array, the
`pondContours` key completeness and its LRU behaviour, the raised `_detMemo` ceiling, and the four rejections.
Three pre-existing source-shape guards (`wseSensitivity`, `pondV3PrD`, `pondV3PrR5`) were updated to the
refactored source with their INTENT unchanged and the reason recorded inline at each.

### B1154 — Right-click "Add control point" missed wherever the road CURVED: the hit test projected onto the chords, not the road `[Site Planner / roads]` (bug) #site-planner #road #ui  *(owner chat block 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-1, with a root-caused diagnosis: "I tried right clicking and I can't extend the road for whatever reason, but if I try and click on a different portion of it then it does work, so it's kinda iffy." Minted **B1154** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`. Branch `claude/road-curve-hit-test-u74avz`. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done for `hitEditPath` / `projToSeg` / `insertRoadVertex` / "control point": **B230** built the shared vertex-editing hit test, **B718** taught it about centerline roads and gave roads their wide pavement tolerance, **B872** added the dock-wall refusal. None of them projects onto anything but the chords, and none is a fix that failed to stick — this is the net-new curved case they all share.)* *(RENUMBERED on merge: minted B1149/B1150/V533 against a fresh `origin/main`, but the B779 mint gate found B1153/V534 already claimed on other in-flight branches — the documented late-bind race, caught RED before merge exactly as designed. Landed at **B1154 / B1155 / V535**, leaving a gap because a gap is free and a second renumber pass is not. Code, tests and the harness carry the provisional NEW-1/NEW-2 labels throughout, so only heading lines moved.)*
`[x]` **DONE — sandbox-verified 2026-07-30 (Verify: sandbox).** Driven through the REAL render path on the owner's REAL geometry: right-clicking the apex of the truck loop's 120 ft return on Tsakiris / Concept A now offers "Add control point" (it did not before), and the insertion hint appears with it.
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **Root cause, exactly as the owner's brief traced it.** `hitEditPath` found an edge with `projToSeg(fp, path.pts[i], path.pts[i+1])` — the straight CHORD between consecutive control points — with a tolerance of about the strip half-width, on the stated reasoning that "a click anywhere on the pavement hits the centerline". That reasoning holds only while the centerline IS the chord. The pavement is generated from `roadDenseCenterline` → `roadCenterline`, which builds a CURVED alignment from each vertex's treatment, and on a bend the chord cuts the corner. **Measured on the owner's own plan:** the apex of `e38duuwgj`'s 120 ft return (a ~91° bend on a 40 ft road) stands **35.8 ft** from the nearest chord against a **20.5 ft** tolerance — unreachable at any zoom, because both terms scale together. So no edge hit, no menu item, and the road's own element menu opened instead. Straight runs still worked: precisely the "works on some portions, not others" he described.
- **Fix — hit-test the road the renderer DRAWS.** `roadGeometry.js` gains `roadCenterlineTagged`, which returns the dense polyline PLUS, for each dense segment, the control-point segment that owns it; `projectToPolyline` and `projectToRoadCenterline` sit on top and return `{ index, pt, d }` — `index` being exactly the `edgeIndex` `insertRoadVertex` already expects, and `pt` a point ON the drawn centerline. `roadCenterline` is now a thin wrapper over the tagged builder, so its output is unchanged byte for byte (asserted on four of the owner's real roads).
- **All three paths corrected together, so they cannot disagree on a curve.** `editablePath` hands the road path its own `projectEdge`, which `hitEditPath` uses in place of the chord loop — that one seam serves the right-click menu, the Shift-click LEFT-click insert, and the hover insertion hint (`onCanvasVtxMoveCapture`), so the dot appears exactly where a right-click would actually take. The tolerance is untouched, so a click anywhere on the pavement still lands. `startRoadBranch` (B1067's "branch a road from here") got the same correction: it projected onto the chords too, which is how a branch came to be welded to a point the road does not pass through — the other half of B1155.
- **Guards (`test/roadCurvedJunction.test.js`, 17 cases).** A click on the outside of a 120 ft bend, further from BOTH chords than the half-width, now returns an edge hit at the clicked distance; the returned insertion point lies on the drawn centerline to 1e-6; the hit maps to a segment `insertRoadVertex` accepts and splices there; and a SHARP road matches the old chord projection to nine decimal places on index, point and distance — the "byte-identical on an uncurved road" requirement, asserted rather than assumed. Plus the degenerate cases (2-point road, 1-point road, null input).
- **Sandbox evidence.** `npm test` 6520 green · lint 0 errors · build green · `ui-audit/verify-road-split-curved.mjs` Part B drives a real click + right-click on the owner's Tsakiris plan through the built app: **before — "Add control point": NO; after — YES**, with the insertion hint shown.
### B1147 — Pond labels escape the outline on one pond and vanish on another: fit was tested against the bounding box, and "doesn't fit" could end in silence `[Site Planner / map · labels]` (bug) #site-planner #ui #pond  *(owner chat block 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-1 — Goose Creek / "Plan 1 (copy)", City of Baytown, Harris County (project `smqfy48tlk9j`, plan `sms69x8rb2qk`): "the pond labels have just completely disappeared from the southern pond, and then the northern pond is just for some reason showing up outside of the pond." Minted **B1147** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`. Reproduced from the REAL drawn geometry pulled from the production database, not a fixture. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across the whole label/leader/declutter family (**B121** the LOD + collision engine and its rounds 2–4, **B951** parcel badges as obstacles, **B195** the trailer strip's no-leader overflow, **B123** the building stack, **B149**/**B942** the detail tier, **B911** the shared dim font scale, **B1016** the pond-parameter tier, **B1085** the export label frame, **B1088** contour label re-roll, **B1140–B1143** hover-tag offset and pointer accuracy): every one of those tunes WHEN a label shows or how big it is; none of them owns WHETHER it fits its shape or what happens when it does not. Net-new, and it reuses the existing leader + declutter machinery rather than forking a pond-specific path.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30 — live-verified HERE against the real plan (Verify: live, no `Blocker:` remains).** Both ponds are labelled at every zoom step, the label sits inside the outline wherever the pond is drawn wide enough to hold its own name, and the exported PDF sheet names both.
- Verify: live — zoom-/data-density-dependent rendering AND PDF/export parity, both mandatory-live classes. **Done here, not deferred:** `ui-audit/verify-pond-label-fit.mjs` drives the real plan logged-out across a five-step zoom sweep and exports the sheet; no `Blocker:` remains (no auth, no external GIS, real project data seeded locally). See the verification note at the end.
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat (NEW-1).

**AUDIT-FIRST — what each pond actually did, and why the owner's diagnosis is half the story.**
The owner's theory ("the label is too wide to be within the pond") names the TRIGGER correctly. It does not
explain the disappearance, and the two symptoms are not two bugs. Measured against the real rings on the
pre-fix build (`verify-pond-label-fit.mjs`, all five zoom steps):

| | northern `e1454719dshobp` | southern `e1454718dshobp` |
|---|---|---|
| drawn size | 374 ft × 1,083 ft, 6.11 ac | 672 ft × 1,520 ft, 17.03 ac |
| pre-fix, every zoom step | **leadered OUTSIDE** | **leadered OUTSIDE**, and **GONE** at the closest step |

So BOTH ponds took the same branch. The old chain tested the wide `footprint … ac · … sf` line against the
pond's BOUNDING BOX; the northern pond's box is 374 ft wide and the line does not fit at working zoom or
below, so it was pushed out. The southern pond's box is wide enough to pass at inspect zoom but not once
zoomed out, so it followed. What made the southern one *disappear* is what happened NEXT: out on the paper
the label joins the general collision pool, and the old chain's last resort there was to say nothing. One
trigger, two endings — and the ending that says nothing is the defect class this repo keeps fixing.

Two further facts the bounding-box test hid. A bounding box **overstates** an irregular pond's room (these
two fill 66% and 73% of theirs), so a label could be told it fitted when the interior could not hold it.
And the 20.20-ac parcel badge's centroid lands INSIDE the southern pond — a fixed obstacle (B951) sitting
on the only anchor the label was ever allowed to use, because the old chain had exactly one position.

**The fix — an ordered ladder, measured against real room.**
- New shared pure module `lib/labelFitLadder.js` (see B1148). `interiorFitter(ring)` rasterises the ring
  and enumerates the maximal inscribed axis-aligned rectangles, answering "does this label fit, and WHERE"
  against room that exists. `labelForms(lines)` turns a priority-ordered line list into the ordered rungs.
- The ladder, first that FITS the measured interior: **(a)** the current single line · **(b)** STACKED —
  acreage and square footage on their own lines, the owner's ask · **(c)** ABBREVIATED — keep the acreage,
  drop the square footage · **(d)** OUTSIDE with a leader back to the pond · declutter/hide remains a
  COLLISION decision only, never the end of a width test.
- **ASPECT-AWARE by construction.** Rungs are TRIED in order but CHOSEN by measured fit, so stacking (which
  is narrower but TALLER) is never preferred on principle. Verified on a long-thin pond, which keeps the
  single line, and a tall-narrow one, which stacks (`test/pondLabelFit.test.js`).
- A label may also SLIDE within the interior to clear an obstacle — which is what lets the southern pond
  keep its anchor region despite the parcel badge parked on its centroid.
- The pond footprint line is now authored as a reflowable `{parts, sep, keep}` spec (`footprintLabelLine`),
  shared by both call sites. Same words, same two facts; it is simply no longer pre-joined into a string
  with no rungs left to take. `Holds … ac-ft usable · …′ rim to floor` and the `+X ac · +Y sf` added-ground
  line got the same treatment.
- `mustLabel` marks a pond: it may never end a frame unnamed. Its outside placement walks around and
  outward until it clears, and commits rather than going silent.
- Five copies of the same ring-bounding-box loop (three of them inline IIFEs) collapsed to one
  `ringSpanFt` / `ringMinSpanFt` — smaller, and one thing to fix. This is the optimization that pays for
  the new module's bytes: `perf-bundle-audit` is back inside every ceiling.

**Result on the real plan (after).** Both ponds labelled at every zoom step. Eight of ten steps place the
label INSIDE the outline; the two that leader out are the northern pond at wide zoom, where the pond draws
narrower on screen than its own name — rung (d), correctly, with a leader. The exported PDF sheet names
both ponds (PDF-PARITY, asserted on the composed sheet SVG, not inferred).

**No regression.** Tsakiris / Concept A and Bain / Concept A pond rings (also pulled from production) are
asserted corner-by-corner to stay inside their outlines, and the live harness confirms Tsakiris on the real
page. Its label now takes the STACKED rung — the wide line never actually fitted its interior, only its
bounding box.

- Files: `lib/labelFitLadder.js` (new) · `lib/labelLayout.js` · `SitePlanner.jsx` · `test/labelFitLadder.test.js` (new) · `test/pondLabelFit.test.js` (new) · `test/fixtures/gooseCreekPonds.json` (new, real geometry) · `ui-audit/verify-pond-label-fit.mjs` (new) · `ui-audit/fixtures/goose-creek-plan1copy.json` (new, the real plan) · `test/pondV3PrQ.test.js` · `MAP.md` · the Site Planner folder pointer.
- ✅ **Verified live 2026-07-30** — headless Chromium against the real Goose Creek plan seeded logged-out: five-zoom sweep, both ponds present at every step, PDF export names both, Tsakiris unmoved. Full suite 6,473 green · lint 0 errors · build green · bundle budgets green · MAP/doc-pointer/panel-copy audits green.

### B1148 — Make the map-label fit ladder a shared, guarded rule so "no label at all" cannot come back on another element type `[Site Planner / map · labels]` (task) #site-planner #ui #testing  *(owner chat block 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-2 — the follow-on to B1147: "it should not be pond-only and it should not be re-derivable by accident." Minted **B1148** via `--against-main`. DEDUPE-FIRST: the extraction precedent is `pondOptimizeAffordance.js` / `pondVerdict.js`; no existing item covers a shared label-fit rule or its invariant.)*
`[x]` **✅ DONE 2026-07-30 (Verify: sandbox).** The fit/fallback decision lives in one pure module, and one guard test asserts the property that broke.
- Verify: sandbox — a pure module plus its unit guard; nothing here needs a browser.
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat (NEW-2).

- **The module.** `lib/labelFitLadder.js` — `LADDER_RUNGS` (the ordered vocabulary, with deliberately no
  `hidden` rung), `labelForms` / `inlineLines` (the reflow forms), `interiorFitter` / `pointInRing` (the
  polygon interior measurer). Pure geometry, no React, no DOM. `labelLayout.js` consumes it; a source guard
  asserts that import, so a future edit cannot quietly re-derive fit beside it.
- **The invariant, stated once and tested:** *a label may be relocated or abbreviated, but a FIT failure
  alone can NEVER produce no label at all.* Hiding stays available to the COLLISION engine as a deliberate
  declutter decision — that is B121/B951 and it is correct — but it is not, and may never be, the end of the
  fit ladder. `test/labelFitLadder.test.js` runs 240 placements (6 hostile shapes × 4 label sets × 5 zooms ×
  2 rotations) with NO obstacles, so nothing can be blamed on a collision, and asserts every one is placed
  with its name line intact and a legal rung; rect elements are covered separately.
- **Which label types consume the ladder, and which deliberately do not:**
  - **Every centred element label goes through it** — it is inside `layoutLabels`, the one collision engine
    the whole canvas and the export sheet share. Buildings, paving, roads, parking, sidewalks, trailer
    strips, ponds and the added-detention label all reflow through the same rungs.
  - **Polygon elements additionally get INTERIOR measurement** (`ring`/`ringOrigin`/`ringPpf`) — ponds,
    drawn polygon buildings/paving, added-ground labels. This is where the bounding box lied.
  - **Rect elements deliberately do NOT** pass a ring: for an axis-aligned or rotated rectangle the bounding
    box IS the interior, so measuring a raster would cost work and buy nothing. They keep their existing
    behaviour exactly.
  - **Ponds alone are `mustLabel`** — a named piece of infrastructure carrying acreage and storage duty may
    not go silent. Buildings and paving deliberately stay declutterable: a dense plan needs the collision
    engine to be allowed to thin the field, and every one of them is identifiable by shape and position in
    a way a pond is not.
  - **Not in scope, deliberately:** the parcel-area badges (a fixed layer that is an obstacle, not a
    reflowable label — B951), the red per-edge dimension numbers (lowest tier, pinned to their footprint by
    B592 and hidden rather than moved), contour labels (their own placement rule, B1088), and the
    Doc Review markup layer (a different canvas with its own model).
- Files: `lib/labelFitLadder.js` · `lib/labelLayout.js` · `test/labelFitLadder.test.js` · the Site Planner folder pointer.
- ✅ **Done 2026-07-30** — module extracted, invariant guarded, source guard green.

### B1144 — The bundle gate fails on rounding errors: every ceiling is pinned to within 0.06% of measured, so any feature trips it `[Infra / CI]` (task) #infra #perf #testing  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-1. Minted **B1144** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done: **B1040** built the budget system, **B1042/B1064** own the bytes, **B1086** withdrew the frame-time seed. None of them is about the ceiling POLICY, which is what fails here. Net-new, not a recurrence.)*
`[x]` **SHIPPED 2026-07-30 — the policy was fixed, not the three numbers.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **The report, measured.** 28 failed runs on `.github/workflows/build.yml`; PR #858 failed 4×, #859 2×, #860 1×. Every one on step 12, `node ui-audit/perf-bundle-audit.mjs`. Lint, the drift guards, `npm test` and the build itself all passed. #860's breaches were **+0.9%** (`siteRouteJsBytes`) and **+0.8%** (`largestChunkBytes`); `totalJsBytes` cleared its ceiling by 3 KB. On `main` at `d5476d0` the largest chunk measured 1707.9 KB against a 1709.0 KB ceiling — **1.1 KB, 0.06% of headroom**. That directly contradicts `perf-budgets.json`'s own stated rule ("seeded from the baseline PLUS headroom, so it is green on day one and only trips on a real regression").
- **⚠ Note for the record: #858 / #859 / #860 had already merged by the time this was picked up** (B1130/B1131 raised the three ceilings by hand on 2026-07-30 — the fourth instance of exactly the failure mode the budget file forbids). So this item did not "unblock" them; it removes the reason a fifth PR would need the same hand-edit.
- **THE FIX IS A POLICY.** A byte metric no longer stores a ceiling. It stores a `baseline` — the last deliberately recorded measurement — and the ceiling is **derived**: `baseline + max(2% of baseline, 32 KB)`, from one committed `bundle.headroom` band rather than three hand-typed numbers that each drift alone. Four outcomes, one red: `≤ target` passes silently · `target…baseline` prints ABOVE TARGET and names the owner · `baseline…ceiling` prints **ABOVE BASELINE** with how much band is left, and **passes** · past the ceiling **fails hard**, printing the derivation and the exact ratchet command.
- **`totalJsBytes` is banded too**, as the brief asked — it had 4.3 KB (0.11%) of headroom and was next in line to surprise someone. Its `target` is kept EQUAL to its baseline so it keeps asserting "no known gap", and the ratchet moves both together so it cannot silently acquire an unowned one.
- **THE RATCHET IS A NAMED STEP WITH TEETH.** `npm run perf:ratchet -- --metric … --item B### --reason "…"` (`scripts/perf-ratchet.mjs`) **measures the value itself from a fresh build** — you cannot ratchet to a number you typed — refuses without an `--item` and a ≥24-character `--reason`, refuses a RAISE without `--allow-raise`, and appends to `bundle.ratchetLog.entries`. It writes **surgically** (one `"baseline": N` line + one log entry), never a `JSON.stringify` round-trip, because this file is one people read. Enforcement: `test/perfBudgetPolicy.test.js` asserts **every baseline equals the `to` of its own latest log entry**, so a baseline edited by hand — with no reason on the record — goes RED in CI. That is what turns "a ceiling ratchets down only when an optimization lands" from an intention into a fact.
- **Proven on both sides of the line, not just described.** The new suite pins that the 0.9% growth which failed #860 now reports and passes, that one byte past the derived ceiling still fails, that the band is `max(2%, 32 KB)` and not the percentage alone, that a chunk COUNT gets no band, and that the ratchet script exits non-zero on a missing item, a missing reason, a four-character reason, and a missing metric.
- **The mechanism was then USED, not just installed:** all three baselines ratcheted **DOWN** in this same PR off the optimizations in B1145 and B1064(a) — `largestChunkBytes` 1702.7 → 1378.9 KB, `siteRouteJsBytes` 2266.3 → 2242.2 KB, `totalJsBytes` 3887.3 → 3886.1 KB — with the reason on the record. **No ceiling was raised anywhere in this work.**
- Docs: `docs/PERF-BUDGETS.md` "Baseline, band, ceiling, target" replaces "Ceilings vs targets", with the outcome table and the ratchet commands.
- Evidence: `npm test` 6483 green (383 files) · lint 0 errors · build green · `node ui-audit/perf-bundle-audit.mjs` green.

### B1145 — Split the map/geometry vendor libraries into their own chunk `[Infra / Build]` (task) #infra #perf #site-planner  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-2. Minted **B1145**. DEDUPE-FIRST: **B1064** explicitly says "do NOT reach for `manualChunks`" — the owner overruled that in part, deliberately and with the honest limit stated; B1064 is amended in place rather than duplicated, and this item owns the change itself.)*
`[x]` **SHIPPED 2026-07-30 — with the limit stated first, because the limit is the interesting part.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO:** it does **not** reduce `siteRouteJsBytes`. The same bytes still download on a Site route — the planner needs leaflet at first paint and clipper at the road-network dissolve. Measured: 2266.3 → 2260.7 KB, which is noise, not a saving. Anyone reading this as "the planner got lighter" has read it wrong.
- **WHAT IT DOES DO, both measured:** `largestChunkBytes` **1702.7 → 1388.8 KB (−313.8 KB)** — that metric measures the biggest INDIVISIBLE unit the browser must parse and compile before anything runs, and splitting a 1.7 MB lump lets that work interleave. And **cache invalidation**: with one chunk, every planner edit re-hashed the file that also holds leaflet + clipper-lib + esri-leaflet + @terraformer, so a returning user re-downloaded ~310 KB of libraries that had not changed. Split out, those bytes keep their hash across a release.
- Deliberately narrow: only the map/geometry closure moves. `react`/`react-dom` stay in the shared entry chunk (on every route, so a separate chunk adds a request without adding cache stability) and nothing app-owned moves at all.
- **⚠ THE TRAP, and it cost a full build cycle to find — written into `vite.config.js` so nobody pays for it twice.** Rollup's CommonJS interop helper (`\0commonjsHelpers.js`) is shared by every chunk that consumes a CJS dependency. Under default chunking it lives in the ENTRY chunk, which every route loads anyway, so it is free. Adding a manual chunk makes that chunk entry-like for rollup's dependent-entry grouping, and because the helper is tiny `experimentalMinChunkSize` then **merges it into the new chunk** — at which point EVERY route statically imports the map vendor bytes to reach a few hundred bytes of interop. Measured on the first attempt: **Review 1248.9 → 1557.1 KB, Library 675.1 → 983.3 KB, Scheduler 553.1 → 861.3 KB.** A straight regression on three routes, invisible unless you look. Pinning the helper to its own `cjs-interop` chunk breaks the merge; final figures are Review +0.3 KB, Library +0.2 KB, Scheduler +0.3 KB — the interop chunk itself and nothing else.
- **A REAL BUG FOUND IN THE MEASURING INSTRUMENT.** `stemOf` stripped `-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}\.js$` — "8 **or more**" hash characters — which silently ate the tail of any HYPHENATED chunk name: `map-vendor-BLBG5Rcw.js` came back as the stem **"map"**, `cjs-interop-…` as **"cjs"**. Both would have gone into the committed allowlist as nonsense names, and `perf-harness.mjs` (which carried its own copy of the same line) reported two expected chunks as phantom intruders. Now matched at exactly 8, and the harness imports the one shared `stemOf` instead of duplicating it.
- **The allowlist guard earned its keep, twice**, failing by NAME on `map-vendor` and again on `teams` before either was admitted. `siteRouteChunks` 4 → 7 and the allowlist +3, each member documented in `perf-budgets.json` with what it contains and why. The sharp guard (fail-by-name) is unchanged; the NEW-9 regression it exists for would still be caught.
- Evidence: `npm test` 6483 green · lint 0 errors · build green · bundle audit green · `node ui-audit/perf-harness.mjs` frame median 16.7 ms / p90 16.7 ms / heap 53.4 MB, all inside budget.

### B1146 — A budget breach must name its cause: attribute bytes to vendor vs app, and diff against the base ref `[Infra / CI]` (task) #infra #perf #testing  *(owner chat 2026-07-30, provisional NEW-3. Minted **B1146**. DEDUPE-FIRST: **B1040** built the audit; nothing existing attributes bytes or compares two builds. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **SHIPPED 2026-07-30.**
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **The report.** A breach printed one sentence — `2286.3 KB exceeds 2265.6 KB by 20.7 KB` — and stopped. That reads identically for a 20 KB feature and a 20 KB dependency bump, so every red run cost somebody a local checkout, a local build and a manual diff before they could even decide *optimize this* vs *this is a dependency, ratchet it deliberately*.
- **Attribution.** `vite.config.js` gains a `chunk-module-stats` plugin that writes `dist/.vite/chunk-modules.json` — each chunk's per-module size, straight out of rollup's own `chunk.modules`. **No new dependency, no extra parse**, and inert at runtime. The audit folds it into **vendor / app-shared / app-route** buckets per route and prints the heaviest dependencies. Honest limit stated where the numbers are produced: rollup reports `renderedLength` (post-tree-shake, **pre**-minify), so every attributed number is SCALED by `on-disk ÷ summed renderedLength` for its chunk — the buckets sum exactly to the real chunk sizes, and the split is proportionally faithful, but no single module's number is a precise minified size.
- **Base-ref diff.** `scripts/perf-base-stats.mjs` resolves the PR's base (or `HEAD^` on a push to main), checks it out into a throwaway git worktree with `node_modules` symlinked, builds it, and snapshots it; `perf-bundle-audit.mjs --compare` then names **which modules and packages moved and by how much**, biggest mover first, plus the per-route bucket deltas. Wired into `build.yml` ahead of the gate step so a failing run's log alone carries the diagnosis. `fetch-depth: 0` added to the checkout, because a depth-1 clone has no base commit to compare against.
- **DIAGNOSIS, NEVER A GATE — by construction.** `perf-base-stats.mjs` exits 0 on every failure path (shallow clone, unresolvable base, a base that does not build, a base predating the stats plugin) and prints the reason. Module ids are made CWD-relative so the base worktree's different path does not make every module look moved. And when the base snapshot has no per-module data, the module/package/bucket sections are **withheld entirely** rather than diffed against nothing — subtracting from an absent base labels every module in the build as new in this PR, which is worse than saying nothing. A diagnostic that can turn a build red is a diagnostic people delete.
- **It paid for itself immediately:** the 4× overstatement of the analysis stack recorded on B1064 came out of this attribution, and so did the finding that `SitePlanner.jsx` alone is 581.2 KB of a 1378.9 KB chunk.
- Evidence: `npm test` 6483 green · lint 0 errors · build green · verified end-to-end locally against `HEAD^` (headline metrics compared, per-module withheld with its reason, exactly as designed for a base that predates the plugin).

I should have the same optionality for any measurement tool or shape that I have for any other shape. Make all the measurement tools have optionality like this." Minted **B1151** via `git fetch origin main && npm run next-id -- --against-main`. Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat. Net-new for the Site Planner.)*
`[x]` **DONE — sandbox-verified 2026-07-30 (Verify: sandbox).** Confirmed in a headless browser in BOTH themes: per-measurement colour, weight, dash, fill and fill opacity paint on the canvas and round-trip through the plan.
- Verify: sandbox
- Origin: filed 2026-07-30 from chat
- **AUDIT-FIRST, what the code actually did.** A measurement was the LAST drawn object with no style of its own. Its colour was hardcoded at the single place it was painted — `const mcolor = warn ? "#b45309" : PAL.accent` — and no measure object carried a `stroke` / `weight` / `dash` / `fill` field anywhere in the model, while a markup shape beside it had the full set reachable from the properties panel. So double-clicking an area measurement opened a panel with nothing to style. The report is exactly right.
- **THE FIX — one resolver, the same editing surface, every mode.** `lib/measureStyle.js` (new, pure) is now the ONE place a measurement's paint is decided: stroke, line weight, line style, and for a closed area a fill colour and fill opacity, for **all four modes** (line · polyline · area · count), not just area. The properties panel reuses the markup panel's own controls — the shared `ColorField` (so measurements inherit the recently-used-colours list), the shared `DASH_OPTIONS` list, the shared live-pick/one-undo-frame writers — rather than standing up a parallel surface.
- **Born with the user's Standards defaults**, the `parcelDefaultStyle` mechanic exactly (B929): `measureDefaultStyle(settings)` is stamped at all four creation sites, a new **Standards → Measurements** section sets them, and the panel's one Apply pushes them onto measurements already drawn (`standardsApply.applyMeasureStandard`, the parcel WRITE mechanic — measurements are stamped, not resolved at render). Ladder: built-in < account default ("Save for all projects") < project default < per-measurement override. A value equal to the built-in is deliberately NOT stamped, so an untouched plan gains no keys and renders byte-identically.
- **THE ONE DELIBERATE EXCEPTION IS PRESERVED, and it is now tested rather than incidental.** When the drawing is UNCALIBRATED the measurement is forced amber over the user's colour — for both the line and the fill — because that is a CORRECTNESS signal ("this number is in raw units, not real feet"), not decoration. The colour is not destroyed, only overridden: it returns the moment the sheet is calibrated, and the panel says so in plain English. The owner rule that a selected measurement carries **no × delete badge** also stands, unchanged.
- **Double-click opens Properties** — verified live rather than assumed; it already worked (`isDoubleTap` in `startMoveMeasure`, B750 parity) and now has a guard so it cannot regress.
- **A SECOND, UNRELATED DEFECT FIXED IN PASSING, found while wiring this.** Every colour chip in these panels was blank: the callers passed a style override containing `background: "var(--surface-raised)"`, which is spread ON TOP of the current colour `ColorField` paints as the chip's background. So the control you click to change a colour showed no colour — in the markup panel and the parcel-drawing panel too, not only the new one. One word removed in three places; guarded.
- **Sandbox evidence.** 31 unit assertions in `test/measureStyle.test.js` — every mode round-trips a FULL style through save and reload, a new measurement picks up the Standards defaults, the built-in resolves to the pre-styling render byte for byte (weight 1.5 / +1 selected, fill 0.10 / +0.06 selected), and the uncalibrated amber still wins over a user colour — plus 22 wiring guards in `test/measureWiring.test.js` and the headless harness `ui-audit/verify-measure-presentation.mjs` (a green dashed heavy run and a violet count both painting their own colour, light and dark, the full control set present in the panel). `npm test` 6547 green · lint 0 errors · build green.
